Sökstuga: Från idé till ansökan – hur tar du nästa steg?

Ett livskraftigt civilsamhälle är en grundpelare för demokrati och mänskliga rättigheter. Samtidigt står många civilsamhällesorganisationer i Sverige inför växande utmaningar: ökade samhällsbehov, större utsatthet hos målgrupper och ett mer komplext omvärldsläge. Frågan om finansiering har därför blivit allt mer central för civilsamhällets möjlighet att verka, nå ut och bidra till samhällsutvecklingen.

I denna interaktiva sökstuga delar Postkodlotteriets Stiftelse med sig av tips, lärdomar och råd kring hur man utformar en stark ansökan. Tillsammans utforskar vi idéer, diskuterar möjligheter och svarar på frågor.

Välkommen att ta med din idé och få hjälp att ta nästa steg! ✨

vrijdag 13 november 2026 — Winnaarsverhalen, Plus

Een envelop met 10 cheques

Met de bekende gouden envelop onder zijn arm belt Gaston aan bij Nadine. Ze weet nog van niets en is compleet verrast als ze hem ziet staan. Eenmaal binnen haalt Gaston de cheques tevoorschijn. Omdat Nadine met Plus meespeelt op postcode 2342 BG, wint ze 10 jaar lang ieder jaar € 25.000,-."Wauw fantastisch, ik ben helemaal sprakeloos.” 

Een mooi begin op haar nieuwe plek 

En dat geluk komt precies op tijd. Over 3 weken verhuist Nadine naar een nieuwe woning. Als Gaston naar haar wensen vraagt, weet ze het meteen. "Er moet nog een nieuwe eethoek komen. Dat kan nu zeker!", vertelt ze blij. Dat wordt straks extra genieten in haar nieuwe huis. 

Ook kans maken op bijzondere prijzen? 

Met Plus maak je extra kans op mooie prijzen, zoals 10 jaar lang € 25.000,- per jaar. Speel jij al mee met Plus?

Growing food has never been easy. Farmers make decisions every day on things they can’t completely control: Will the rain come on time? Will temperatures stay manageable? Will pests destroy the crops? Is the soil healthy?

There has always been uncertainty, but climate change is making many of those conditions harder to predict. And for farmers operating on small plots, whose work supports businesses and jobs far beyond the farm, those changes can mean smaller harvests and lower incomes.

For example, in sub-Saharan Africa, where around 80% of food is produced by smallholder farmers, the problem is especially pressing. But why does that matter for the rest of us?

How does climate change affect agriculture?

Climate change makes weather more extreme and less predictable, with more heat, drought, flooding, and shifting rainfall. Smallholder farmers often cannot afford tools to protect their crops and animals from floods and droughts. In parts of Africa, worn-out soil, scarce water, and expensive fertilizer can also lead to smaller harvests.

When farming gets harder, the effects don’t stop at the farm

Farms are only the beginning of the food system. A harvest of maize, for example, might start on a farm, then might be sold to a distributor, then to a grocery store or market, and eventually make its way to someone’s kitchen. In fact, around 70–75% of the price consumers pay for food is created after it leaves the farm.

Multiply that journey by all the food we eat and you start to see what a food system really is: an entire network of people, businesses, processors, sellers, and consumers involved in getting food from farm to plate.

In parts of Africa, about half the population depends on primary agriculture — the process of growing crops and raising animals to produce food and other raw materials–for a living. When you include the wider agrifood system, it accounts for roughly two-thirds of all jobs.

So when a farmer has a difficult season, the consequences can ripple outward. The farmer has less food to sell and less income to spend. A trader has less to buy. A transporter has less product to move. Businesses throughout the local area can feel the effects. A shock to a small farm can be a shock to the entire community.

The reverse is also true: When farms become more productive and reliable, those gains can create more income and opportunity throughout the food system. A farmer who sells more can invest in the next season: better seed, a water pump, improved storage, or an extra pair of hands at harvest. Traders, transporters, and shops have more to buy, move, and sell. And across millions of farms, countries can grow more of the food they need and spend less importing it.

Women are especially important to these systems. In sub-Saharan Africa, 76% of working women are employed in agrifood systems. Yet women farmers can face additional barriers in accessing things like land, technology, financing, information, and markets, all of which can make adapting to changing conditions more difficult.

2.69B

In 2025, 2.69 billion people — nearly one-third of the world’s population — could not afford a healthy diet.

Ultimately, what happens on farms affects whether communities have reliable access to nutritious food. In 2025, 2.69 billion people — nearly one-third of the world’s population — could not afford a healthy diet.

Farmers are already finding ways to adapt

There isn’t one solution to helping farmers with climate adaptation. But new tools are making it possible for farmers to make better decisions, protect their harvests and income, and get more from the resources they already have. Here are three examples making a difference:

1 Better information about weather

Farmers have always watched the weather. Now, more precise forecasts can give them better information about what’s coming.

In Kenya, TomorrowNow and the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) are making hyperlocal weather information available to more than 6 million farmers.

That information can help a farmer answer very practical questions like: Is rain likely this week? When is the right time to plant? Better information doesn’t eliminate the risk of a drought or flood. But it can give farmers more time to prepare and protect a season’s worth of income.

2 Crops that can handle tougher conditions

Another approach is developing crops that are better suited to the conditions farmers are experiencing now. Researchers are working with farmers to develop varieties that can better withstand challenges such as drought, heat, pests, and disease.

In Uganda, for example, scientist Dr. Clare Mukankusi at CGIAR, a global research partnership dedicated to a food-secure future, developed new bean varieties to thrive in drier conditions and poorer soil.

For a farmer, a hardier crop can mean the difference between losing most of a harvest and having enough to eat and sell.

3 Better information about soil

Healthy crops also depend on healthy soil. But farmers can’t always tell what their soil needs simply by looking at it. Soil-mapping tools can provide a clearer picture of what is happening beneath the surface and help farmers make more informed decisions about how to manage their land.

In Kenya, a tool called Virtual Agronomist uses digital soil maps to help farmers understand what their soil needs and make better decisions about fertilizer.

Combined with innovations designed to improve soil health, that information can help farmers use limited resources more effectively and keep their land productive.

A more resilient food system

No technology can make agriculture risk-free. But better forecasts, stronger crops, healthier soils, and other innovations, such as irrigation, can give farmers more options as conditions change.

The goal is simple: help farmers produce food more reliably and earn more from what they produce.

When that happens, the benefits can extend well beyond an individual farm. Families can earn more stable incomes. Local businesses can grow. Communities can have more reliable food supplies. And food systems can become better prepared for whatever comes next.

Growing food is becoming more difficult. But farmers, scientists, governments, and businesses are already finding ways to adapt—and getting those solutions into the hands of more farmers can help build a more resilient future for all of us.

Meet Mrs. Ramatu Alhaji Yusuf, a smallholder farmer and community leader in the state of Kano in Northern Nigeria.  

Farmers like Yusuf grow several crops—sorghum, millet, soybeans, tomatoes, and onions. But one of the most important staples in this region is the cowpea. Thanks to new varieties developed by CGIAR—a global agriculture research network—farmers can now grow cowpeas that mature more quickly. Unlike most crops, these improved varieties can be cultivated twice during a growing season that only lasts four months. That means more food for families and more income from market sales. 

Yusuf, who began farming when she was 18 or 19, was introduced to the crop by her husband. The labor-intensive work involves specific roles across the family: men till the soil, while women and children plant and harvest. When Yusuf first started, growers planted local cowpea varieties that were poorly suited to the region’s increasingly unpredictable climate. Frequent droughts, intense heat, flooding, plant disease, and pests led to very poor yields. In recent years, the introduction of more drought- and disease-tolerant cowpea varieties has begun to change that—and more.  

The improved cowpea varieties Yusuf grows today are hardier, faster-growing, and more resistant to pests. That means better growing seasons, and many more products that she can sell at the market. The extra income helps her pay university tuition for two of her children and enroll the other eight in private school. 

There have been changes at home, too. In her traditional Hausa community, women are expected to stay at home when not farming. “Before, you had to wait for your husband to do everything for you,” Yusuf says. “Now, if there’s a problem, I’ll just go solve [it].”

Her leadership has extended beyond the household. After serving for years as a secretary for a local women farmers’ cooperative, Yusuf was appointed chairperson. She began holding meetings with 15 fellow growers to prepare for the cowpea planting season. Today, more than 100 women attend these gatherings.  

But Yusuf still gets into the weeds—literally—visiting each plot where a member intends to plant, assessing the soil quality and suitability. If a plot isn’t viable, she helps find a better one. These hands-on efforts have earned her deep trust in the community.  

“A lot of women have benefitted from cowpea farming,” she says.” Some have bought farmland. Some use the money from cowpea sales to set up [other] businesses that provide another source of income. Others use their profits to sponsor their children’s education [or] wedding ceremonies.”

What Yusuf has built—through hard work, experience, and leadership—goes beyond bigger harvests and higher earnings. In a place where many believe women should not venture far from the home, she breaks norms every day, with her husband’s full support. Whether attending planning meetings or even going door-to-door to connect with other farmers, Yusuf is redefining what’s possible. While she initially experienced disapproval from other women, she’s seen norms shift and opinions change. “Those women saw the benefit in this work, and they came to me and asked to join. They said, ‘We want to achieve what you are achieving.’ ”

“Now if there’s a problem, I’ll just go solve the problem.”

– Mrs. Ramatu Yusuf

Rebecca Jerop believes that the future of Kenyan agriculture requires a return to its roots: traditional crops that once sustained communities but have since been largely overlooked.

As an agricultural economist and lecturer at Laikipia University, Jerop is working to ensure that agricultural innovations—from soil conservation practices and climate-resilient seeds to marketing initiatives—work for smallholder farmers, many of whom are being forced to adapt to a changing climate. What approaches are most cost effective? What can build long-term sustainability? And, crucially, what can help farmers not just survive but thrive?

For Jerop, one of the most promising ways to build a more climate-resilient future is to reintroduce an ancient grain: finger millet. Once a staple of Kenyan diets, this nutrient-dense cereal is rich in calcium and vitamins and thrives in harsh, dry conditions. In regions where drought and degraded soils have made farming more precarious, finger millet stands out—not only for its resilience but also for its potential to improve nutrition, incomes, and economic stability in farming communities that are most at risk.

By helping to reintroduce crops like finger millet, Jerop is connecting economics, traditions, and innovation in a way that could reshape the future of farming in Kenya—and far beyond. We spoke with Jerop about her journey to this work, the promise of traditional crops in climate change adaptation, and her vision for food security in Kenya.

“They don’t need to be told about climate change; they know it…”

– Dr. Rebecca Jerop

A long time ago, my parents grew finger millet. It was a common food in my village. But at some point, these kinds of crops started disappearing and you saw only maize. There were new varieties of maize at the time, and they were simple to grow compared to finger millet. Early on, production was high. But maize became less productive in this region over time because of climate change. It wasn’t resilient to drought, so the crop could be wiped out and farmers would have nothing. It requires a lot of fertilizer, which causes the soil to become acidic. So it’s no longer sustainable. When I began my research work, I remembered the traditional crops, and I began thinking again about finger millet.

Finger millet doesn’t need much space, especially compared to maize. For maize to be economically viable, you have to produce it on a large scale. But in Kenya, the largest plots of land in most places are just 0.2 or 0.3 hectares [about half the size of a soccer field]. Finger millet is a short-season crop, so you can grow two or even three crops per year. It’s nutritious. In my village, it was a common food for pregnant women and young children. Finger millet will do well even in a drought.

I believe these underutilized crops are very good crops, and I want to figure out how we can get them back to farmers. A big problem is they had been neglected in the research. Finger millet had a problem long ago with low yields, but more researchers began working on it. There’s a lot more innovation, and a lot of new varieties that are more productive. With the new varieties, we also have some ways where we can conserve the soil and water. So I’m looking at different initiatives to see if they’re efficient, if they increase productivity. Have farmers adopted these innovations? If not, why not? Is there any impact on productivity? Or on commercialization? If you commercialize these crops—as opposed to growing for subsistence—and the farmers get income from them, they can continue embracing the crops.

There are many challenges, but the first one is consumer awareness. Farmers need to market this crop because it has a lot of benefits compared to maize. For one thing, it’s a very nutritious crop. After awareness, there’s also the issue of processing. During harvest season, we have processing companies that come and buy the maize. But with finger millet, processing is more challenging. Another issue is that farmers may need to be trained in how to increase productivity and be able to access the market.

I think most of the farmers are aware of certain changes. They don’t need to be told about climate change—they know it from their experiences. They can tell you how, some years back, they were sure when the planting season would start, when to expect the rains, and how long the rains would last. Not anymore. Farmers are seeing changing weather patterns, and they’re not sure when to plant, what to grow. That’s what they’re talking about. They’re looking at planting short-season crops and are interested in drought resistance. Because of growing awareness, you see more farmers growing finger millet, not as a major crop yet, but as part of their diversification.

I believe food insecurity may be increasing because of issues around climate change. But these traditional crops, especially finger millet, are well adapted to the local environment. They will do well as the climate changes. If we adopt this crop, we will have a more resilient food system. We also have the issue of malnutrition here. If we can encourage farmers to grow these crops, which are very nutritious, we can alleviate some of that. People are becoming more aware of the benefits of these underutilized crops. But it’s a slow process. I hope one day farmers will fully embrace these crops and have an impact on nutrition and food security.

Jerop’s work is a reminder that innovation doesn’t always mean something new. Sometimes, the future lies in remembering what once worked—and bringing it back to help people thrive.

Gaston is op bezoek in Amersfoort. Op postcode 3823 BR valt de PostcodeStraatprijs: 9 deelnemers winnen € 25.000,- per lot. Zodra de gouden enveloppen opengaan, komen de reisplannen op tafel. En zoals altijd heeft Gaston ook een gloednieuwe BMW bij zich. 

maandag 9 november 2026 - Winnaarsverhalen

Een huis vol koeien 

Gaston belt eerst aan bij Jeannette. Zij verzamelt alles wat met koeien te maken heeft. Maar Gaston komt voor iets anders. Hij geeft haar een gouden envelop en Jeannette is dolblij met haar cheque. Wat ze ermee gaat doen? “Een nieuwe elektrische fiets. Die gaat er nu komen!” 

Op naar verre oorden

Samen lopen ze naar buiten, waar de buren al wachten. Tegelijk gaan de enveloppen open. Joske wint € 25.000,- en weet het meteen: “Ik wil met mijn zoon op safari. In Namibië of Kenia.” Ton en Marel winnen samen € 75.000,-. Waar ze heen gaan, weten ze nog niet. “Maar we gaan zeker samen op reis.” 

Niet thuis, maar wel de BMW gewonnen 

Dan is er nog die ene verrassing: de gloednieuwe BMW. Alleen is de winnaar niet thuis. Het team van de Postcode Loterij brengt het goede nieuws later alsnog. Wat een verrassing!

Kijk uit voor mails waarin wordt aangegeven dat je een fiets gewonnen zou hebben. Het probleem is bij ons bekend en wordt onderzocht. 

donderdag 15 oktober 2026 - Algemeen

We adviseren mensen om niet op links in verdachte e-mails te klikken en altijd het volledige e-mailadres van de afzender en het webadres achter een link te controleren. 

  • Onze juiste naam: Postcode Loterij (dus zonder Nationale). Deze naam staat altijd in ons mailadres. 

  • De officiële website van de Postcode Loterij: www.postcodeloterij.nl.

     

Wij hebben wel links in onze mails staan, maar zullen niet vragen om geld over te maken. Twijfel je over de echtheid van een e-mail? Klik niet op links in dergelijke e-mails en deel nooit je bankgegevens. Controleer dan altijd de afzender van het bericht en niet alleen de getoonde naam. Vertrouw je het niet en kom je er niet uit? Neem dan contact op met onze Ledenservice. Meer informatie over wat je kan doen als je een phishing e-mail hebt ontvangen, vind je op www.fraudehelpdesk.nl.

A conversation about building Black trans-led creative ecosystems at GIA.

On October 18-21, 2026, the Reva and David Logan Foundation sent three staff members to the Grantmakers in the Arts’ annual conference. The conference, titled “As the South Goes…” (W.E.B. DuBois), took place in Memphis, Tennessee. One of the South’s Mississippi River cities, Memphis, known as the home of Blues and Rock N Roll, has been pivotal in shaping not only the nation’s music but its social movements as well. 

This year’s conference was a unique opportunity to showcase how cultural infrastructure is built and sustained under uneven conditions, and how value moves through sound, migration, ownership, and narrative. Across plenaries, conversations with arts leaders and funders, and visits to cultural organizations throughout Memphis, attendees saw a thriving southern city that continues to model what it means to build a movement toward an abundant arts ecosystem. Here are the reflections from our staff members.

Jessie Mott, Senior Program Officer:

Throughout the conference, I was reminded that a thriving arts ecosystem requires more than funding individual projects. It requires the support of infrastructure that allows artists, organizations, and communities to build relationships, take risks, develop leadership, and sustain their work over time. Changing the conditions that make collective work possible. What if we treated relationships as essential infrastructure rather than a byproduct of our work?

At the National Civil Rights Museum, the conversation about building Black trans-led creative ecosystems brought these ideas into particular focus. The discussion with Elijah McKinnon, Imara Jones, and Joie Shakur connected cultural infrastructure to questions of safety, representation, data sovereignty, and the power of storytelling. In a context where violence is reinforced by dehumanization, art and media can help restore humanity, create connection, and make other futures imaginable. The idea that the ecosystem is the strategy stayed with me.

Jessica Jones-Lewis, Program Officer:

One of the central lessons I took away from the conference was developing a clearer vision for arts in and as place. In learning more about Crosstown Concourse, previously a Sears Distribution Center, it is clear that while creating/repurposing a new space for the arts is important, it also needs to be accessible for the community. These spaces cannot be conceived of or built in a vacuum. 

At showtime, arts organizations welcome the community into their performance venue. But once the show ends, what else does the community get from the space? Can they get a community meeting space? A place for indoor artist or farmers markets during inclement weather? Can alderpeople, politicians or guest speakers use the space for community events? Can schools host performances on the same stages as Chicago’s best artists? Can some of Chicago’s most vulnerable community members find a cooling station in the heat or a warming station in the biting cold? In short, what do our buildings do when the show is over? How could more community invitations result in more resilient communities and more resilient arts spaces?

Sabrina Boggs, Senior Administrator:

The term “middle-class artists” came up on the first day and really stuck with me. In regards to an artist’s career, “middle-class” might imply they are in between early-career and “Beyoncé.” Broadly, however, “middle-class” implies an ability to live comfortably with room for hobby and pleasure. This type of financial stability is most often out of reach for professional working artists.

Despite being massively undervalued, these artists are the pipeline that create Beyoncé. They are her first vocal coach; they are the marching band that inspired her Homecoming tour. Deeply rooted in their communities, they often have the highest touch and highest impact on the next generation of artists and our world in general. They deserve to be middle-class and, beyond that, to create generational wealth. Instead, many of them cobble together multiple jobs to make ends meet, with no health benefits or retirement savings.
 
Unfortunately, funders continue to struggle with how to get artists’ basic needs met. Some funders struggle to pay them at all. In speaking with an anonymous funder at the conference, I learned that they have advocated every year to pay visiting artists a $20 stipend for their large-scale public arts festival, and every year their board ultimately offered artists no compensation. How do we convince arts funders that artists deserve to be paid more than the absolute bare minimum, or even paid at all?
 
Or does it transcend what funders can or are willing to do? Does the answer instead lie in artists creating their own infrastructure, mutual aid, and ownership? If so, how can we help them get to that point?

_______________________________________________________________________________

Despite sending our staff home with more questions than answers, the 2026 GIA Conference provided an opportunity to deeply reflect on the arts beyond what is produced, centering the people and places that make the arts and artists possible. Memphis showed that “The South Got Something to Say!”

Staff members Jessie Mott, Sabrina Boggs, and Jessica Jones-Lewis on Beale Street.

Menno is het liefst buiten. Regelmatig gaat hij samen met zijn broer het water op om te zeilen. Maar binnenkort kan hij ook op avontuur met de camper. En dat heeft alles te maken met zijn postcode: 1474 JK. Én met zijn Premium loten.

donderdag 5 november 2026 — Winnaarsverhalen, Premium

Dubbel geluk in Oosthuizen

Winston komt bij Menno langs met fantastisch nieuws. Samen stappen ze de regen in. Een paar meter verderop staat een prachtige Carado T338 Pro camper op hem te wachten. Menno straalt van oor tot oor! De pakketten worden namelijk ingepakt door mensen die een nieuw bestaan opbouwen in Nederland. Zoals Amani en Jannet, voor wie dit werk veel meer betekent dan alleen een baan. 

donderdag 5 november 2026 - Algemeen

Een plek om te groeien

Bij de Sociale Inpak Club in Amsterdam krijgen mensen die naar Nederland zijn gevlucht de kans om aan hun toekomst te werken. Ze verdienen vier dagen per week hun eigen geld met het inpakken van pakketten. De vijfde dag volgen ze Nederlandse les of krijgen ze hulp bij het solliciteren. Zo leren ze nieuwe vaardigheden en zetten ze stappen richting een zelfstandig bestaan.

Een nieuwe start voor Jannet en Amani

Jannet vluchtte uit Uganda omdat ze daar niet veilig kon leven vanwege haar geaardheid. Nu voelt ze zich thuis bij de Sociale Inpak Club. "Het is echt geweldig om hier te werken", vertelt ze. Ze droomt van een baan in de beautywereld. Ook Amani bouwt aan haar toekomst. Ze vluchtte met haar gezin voor de oorlog en wil graag kleuterjuf worden.

Veel statushouders willen graag aan het werk en hun plek vinden in de samenleving. Wat veel mensen niet weten, is dat statushouders met een inkomen ook een verplichte bijdrage betalen aan hun opvang in een azc. Bij de Sociale Inpak Club krijgen ze de kans om werkervaring op te doen, Nederlands te leren en zorgen voor een inkomen. Zo groeien ze stap voor stap naar een zelfstandige toekomst.

En soms maakt zelfs de prijs al een wereld van verschil. Zoals het (H)eerlijk Pakket, waarmee we Nederlandse impactmakers steunen en mensen nieuwe kansen bieden. Zo brengt één pakket op meerdere plekken plezier. Dat is The Power of Postcodes.

Wat als je door een overstroming ineens niet meer genoeg te eten hebt? Voor veel mensen in Bangladesh is dit de harde werkelijkheid. Huizen lopen onder water en gezinnen verliezen hun inkomen. Juist dan is snelle hulp van levensbelang. Dankzij de steun van de Postcode Loterij helpt het World Food Programme (WFP) mensen in nood. Zoals Halima, die weer hoop kreeg op een betere toekomst. 

donderdag 5 november 2026 - Goede doelen

Een overstroming maakt alles nog moeilijker

Halima woont met haar zoon, die een beperking heeft, in Bangladesh. Als weduwe moest ze bedelen om rond te komen. Toen in 2024 grote overstromingen haar huis bereikten, werd de situatie nog moeilijker. "Er kwam water in ons huis. We konden niet goed koken en hadden te weinig te eten", vertelt ze.

Van noodhulp naar nieuwe kansen

Via het WFP ontving Halima eerst 6.000 taka, de munteenheid van Bangladesh, om eten en andere dagelijkse kosten te betalen. Later kreeg ze een training en 20.000 taka om zelf inkomsten te verdienen. Daarmee kocht ze twee geiten, die ze nu fokt om later te verkopen. Zo bouwt Halima stap voor stap aan een zelfstandig bestaan. "Het heeft ons leven gered", vertelt ze.

Hulp waar die het hardst nodig is

Het WFP helpt wereldwijd mensen die te maken krijgen met honger en noodsituaties. Dankzij flexibele steun van de Postcode Loterij kan de organisatie snel handelen waar de nood het hoogst is. In 2025 hielp deze steun onder andere in Bangladesh, waar veel Rohingya-vluchtelingen afhankelijk zijn van voedselhulp. Ondanks financiële uitdagingen kon het WFP de voedselhulp aan deze gemeenschap op peil houden.

Samen geven we hoop

Het verhaal van Halima laat zien hoeveel verschil hulp op het juiste moment maakt. Dankzij onze deelnemers steunt de Postcode Loterij organisaties zoals het WFP. Zo helpen we samen mensen in nood, dichtbij en ver weg. Met voedsel voor vandaag én nieuwe kansen voor morgen. Dat is de kracht van samen. Dat is The Power of Postcodes.

Elke dag kilometers lopen voor water. Voor veel vrouwen en meisjes in Afrika is dit de dagelijkse werkelijkheid. Het kost veel tijd en energie, die ze niet aan school of werk kunnen besteden. Maar het kan ook anders. Met zanddammen zorgt The Hunger Project ervoor dat water langer beschikbaar blijft. Dankzij de steun van de Postcode Loterij helpt de organisatie dorpen aan water. En dat verandert levens, zoals dat van Aiefa Domingo uit Malawi.

donderdag 5 november 2026 - Goede doelen

Meer tijd voor andere dingen

Aiefa Domingo woont in Julayi, een dorp in Malawi. Voorheen kostte alleen de wandeling naar de boorput haar al anderhalf uur, heen en terug. In het droge seizoen moest ze daar ook nog lang wachten. Nu haalt ze water om te wassen bij een handpomp vlakbij de nieuwe zanddam. En bij de boorput zijn de wachtrijen veel korter. Zo houdt Aiefa elke dag kostbare tijd over.

Een slimme oplossing voor watertekort

Met het project Water Winnen bouwt The Hunger Project samen met Sand Dams Worldwide zanddammen in Malawi, Benin en Burkina Faso. Deze dammen vangen regenwater op en slaan het op in de zandige rivierbedding. Zo blijft er ook tijdens droge periodes water beschikbaar. De inwoners bouwen en onderhouden de dammen zelf. Dat zorgt niet alleen voor water dichtbij, maar ook voor nieuwe kansen.

Samen bouwen aan een betere toekomst

Aiefa hielp zelf mee aan de bouw van de zanddam. Ze bereidde eten voor iedereen op de bouwplaats. Ook volgde ze trainingen over hygiëne, vrouwenrechten en gelijkwaardigheid. Zo leert ze hoe ze gezonder en zelfstandiger kan leven. Het project Water Winnen wil uiteindelijk 12.000 mensen toegang geven tot water voor dagelijks gebruik en landbouw.

Jouw deelname maakt verschil

Het verhaal van Aiefa laat zien hoeveel verschil toegang tot water maakt. Dankzij onze deelnemers steunt de Postcode Loterij goede doelen als The Hunger Project. Samen geven we mensen de kans om hun leven te verbeteren. Van water dichtbij tot meer tijd voor school, werk en een betere toekomst. Dat is de kracht van samen. Dat is The Power of Postcodes.

De zon schijnt in Halsteren, en 9 buren krijgen nóg een reden om te stralen. Op postcode 4661 BS valt de PostcodeStraatprijs: € 25.000,- per lot. Gaston deelt de gouden enveloppen persoonlijk uit. En er staat nog een extra verrassing klaar. 

woensdag 4 november 2026 - Winnaarsverhalen

Al 62 jaar samen

Gaston belt eerst aan bij Bertus en Annie. “We zijn al 62 jaar samen”, vertellen ze lachend. Als Gaston de cheque van € 25.000,- laat zien, wordt hun glimlach nog breder. Bertus is morgen jarig. “We kunnen een feestje geven. En de kinderen zijn hier ook heel blij mee.” Het eerste verjaardagscadeau is binnen. 

Terug naar Suriname

Dan zijn Robert en Wilma aan de beurt. Zodra ze € 25.000,- op hun cheque zien, vallen ze elkaar in de armen. Ze weten al wat ze gaan doen. Een paar jaar geleden reisden ze naar Suriname om de as van Roberts moeder uit te strooien. “We willen graag weer naar Suriname”, vertelt Wilma. 

Samen voor een schone kust en zee

De actie brengt meer dan een opgeruimd strand. Vrijwilligers, regiocoördinatoren, strandpaviljoens en organisaties zetten samen de schouders eronder. Zo groeit een gemeenschap van mensen die zich betrokken voelt bij de kust en de Noordzee. Owen ziet ieder jaar bekende én nieuwe gezichten terug.

Een auto voor de kleinzoon 

Inmiddels staan alle winnaars samen op straat. Gaston geeft het signaal en de enveloppen gaan open. Buren knuffelen elkaar en de eerste plannen komen op tafel. Gerrit en Jacqueline zijn er snel uit: “We willen een nieuwe auto. De oude geven we aan onze kleinzoon. Die heeft net zijn rijbewijs!”  

Dat wordt een bijzondere thuiskomst

Dan heeft Gaston nóg een verrassing. Hij haalt de sleutels van een gloednieuwe BMW tevoorschijn. Maar de winnaar is er niet. Die geniet nog van een vakantie en weet van niets. Wat een thuiskomst wordt dat!

The following first appeared in the Global Peace Almanac. The opinions expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily represent the views of the Rockefeller Brothers Fund.

In an interview with the Global Peace Almanac, Rockefeller Brothers Fund Peacebuilding Program Director Perry Cammack discusses why experimentation is an essential ingredient of social change and how the peacebuilding sector can embrace risk, protect what works, and remain grounded in clear values. 

Q: The peacebuilding field often says it uses evidence to guide its work. From your perspective as a funder, when does evidence genuinely shape decisions, and when does it mainly serve reporting or signaling purposes? And when it does shape decisions, what does that typically look like in practice?

A:  I understand peacebuilding to encompass an extraordinary range of human activities from the hyperlocal, like reducing violence in a school or neighborhood, to the global, like efforts to mediate international conflicts. Peacebuilding practitioners, in whatever context they are working, can certainly benefit from analytical frameworks to shed light on what interventions will be successful. The more these frameworks are tested against real-world experience, the better.

Read the full interview in The Global Peace Almanac.

vrijdag 23 oktober 2026 - Winnaarsverhalen

Verjaardagsverrassing

Gaston belt eerst aan bij jarige Raymond en zijn vrouw Cindy. “Is dit echt?”, vraagt Raymond als hij € 25.000,- op de cheque ziet. Buiten staan de buren al te wachten, en al zingend verwelkomen ze de jarige job. Dan gaan overal de gouden enveloppen open: sommigen winnen € 25.000,-, anderen met meerdere loten € 50.000,- of zelfs € 75.000,-. 

Oude belofte, nieuwe droom

Alex wint € 50.000,-, en dochter Fenna heeft meteen een plan. “Mijn vader beloofde vroeger dat ik een paard zou krijgen als hij de loterij zou winnen”, vertelt ze. “Ja, dat wordt onderhandelen”, lacht Alex. Zeker is wel dat hij met zijn vrouw een mooie reis gaat boeken voor hun 25-jarig huwelijk. Ook Harry en Maria, bijna 50 jaar getrouwd, winnen € 50.000,-. “Komt dat even mooi uit!”, aldus Harry. 

De kers op de (verjaardags)taart

En dan is daar de laatste verrassing. Gaston loopt naar Raymond toe met een sleutel in zijn hand. “Raymond, jij wint ook nog de auto!” “Dit is het mooiste verjaardagscadeau ooit”, zegt hij stralend.

Wat begint als een gewone zondagavond, eindigt voor Geert uit Haren met een geweldige verrassing! In de laatste aflevering van Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht wint Marco uit Riethoven € 480.000,-. En dat betekent dat ook een thuiswinnaar dit bedrag wint. Terwijl Geert nietsvermoedend met hond Senna voetbal kijkt, staat ineens Winston voor de deur. Met een gouden koffer vol goed nieuws! 

woensdag 21 oktober 2026 - Winnaarsverhalen

Een telefoontje op het juiste moment 

Winston en Geert nemen plaats op de bank. Geert woont hier samen met zijn vrouw en zoon, maar vanavond zijn ze toevallig geen van beiden thuis. Maar dan gaat de telefoon! Het is dochter Jessica. Zij ziet haar vader live op tv en wil natuurlijk niets missen. Ze blijft aan de lijn terwijl Winston de gouden koffer opent en het bedrag erop schrijft: € 480.000,-. 

Nieuwe hardloopschoenen

“Onvoorstelbaar, geweldig, dankjewel zeg!”, roept Geert uit. Ook dochter Jessica kan het nauwelijks geloven. “Dit is toch niet normaal!”, klinkt het door de telefoon. En wat gaat Geert met zijn geld doen? Eerder vertelde hij lachend dat hij wel nieuwe hardloopschoenen kan gebruiken. “Die gaan er komen”, belooft Winston.

Ook feest bij de buren

En het feest in Haren is nog niet voorbij. Ook andere deelnemers met 9753 JT vallen in de prijzen. Zij ontvangen bedragen tussen de € 36.923,- en € 73.846,-, afhankelijk van het aantal loten waarmee ze meespelen. Omdat Geert met meerdere loten meespeelt, komt er voor hem nog eens bijna € 37.000,- bovenop de € 480.000,-.

Press Releases

Located between Russia and China, Mongolia has a crowded media landscape. There are 389 active outlets for a population of 3.5 million, all competing fiercely for limited advertising revenue. A new learning brief from the International Fund for Public Interest Media (IFPIM), A catalyst, not a crutch, is a mid-term review of the International Fund’s three-year programme of flexible core funding and strategic support in Mongolia, which runs from December 2023 to December 2026 and is being delivered in partnership with the Nest Center for Journalism Innovation and Development. It draws on the experience of six outlets supported by the International Fund (Graph.mn, iToim, Lemon Press Digital, NTV, UB.life, and Zuunii Medee), setting out what has worked so far, why, and how these lessons might apply to funding public interest media elsewhere.

The early results are striking. In the first 18 months, five of the six grantees increased their non-grant revenue, with a median rise of 23%, compared with 15% across the International Fund’s wider portfolio. This revenue covers, on average, 42% of operating costs. All six improved their operating profit margins, even as costs typically rose by 41% because of new investments. Only three had positive margins at the start, and the cohort median now stands at 32%, against 7% for the wider portfolio. The cohort's workforce also grew by 6%, at a time when many newsrooms worldwide have been shrinking.

These gains came in a challenging environment. Many independent outlets cover their running costs through commercial income, but years of tight margins have left little room to invest in new products, audiences, or technology. Press freedom has also narrowed: Mongolia fell from 68th to 102nd in the Reporters Without Borders (RSF) World Press Freedom Index between 2021 and 2025.

The brief sets out five key insights. The first four explore the factors behind the cohort's performance, and the final one focuses on the enabling conditions that made it possible:

1. Building on solid foundations: flexible funding accelerated growth where the foundations were already in place. Most grantees already ran lean, commercially viable models, so unrestricted funding went into experimentation and strategic investment rather than day-to-day survival. iToim, for example, grew its non-grant revenue by 125% by shifting from one-off contracts to long-term advertising deals with ethical partners.

2. Turning funding into measurable outcomes: diagnostics, planning workshops, monthly check-ins, and performance tracking from FT Strategies and Nest helped outlets set clear, data-driven goals. Grantees cited strategic clarity as one of the programme's main benefits.

3. A trusted local partner: Nest's in-country knowledge shaped the grantee selection, the design of the support package, and legal assistance for outlets facing harassment. This has kept external support closely aligned with the realities of the Mongolian market.

4. Strengthening the wider sector through a cohort: bringing together a diverse group of influential outlets encouraged peer learning, joint reporting, and collective action. This included a coordinated response to a draft Press Freedom Law and shared work on a Mongolian-language AI tool that no single outlet could have built alone.

5. A convergence of favourable conditions: the results reflect commercially capable grantees, a relatively stable media environment, a responsive market with demand for trustworthy journalism, and strong local support. Where organisations face acute financial pressure, the same funding may simply be absorbed into keeping the lights on.

Together, the insights show how flexible funding, combined with strategic and local support, can accelerate the growth of independent media that is already on a sound footing. The findings are not yet final. A fuller picture of the grantees' long-term sustainability will only emerge after the programme ends in December 2026. Still, the Mongolian experience offers a valuable contribution to a pressing question for the sector: what makes funding a catalyst, not a crutch, for independent media?

Download the full learning brief: A catalyst, not a crutch: how flexible funding is strenghtening public interest media in Mongolia

About the learning brief series

This learning brief is part of a series produced by the International Fund's What Works Unit, which documents and analyses the experience of independent media in low- and middle-income countries to understand what works and what does not in responding to the political and structural market challenges facing public interest journalism.

A new learning brief from the International Fund for Public Interest Media (IFPIM), A catalyst, not a crutch, is a mid-term review of the International Fund’s three-year programme of flexible core funding and strategic support in Mongolia, which runs from December 2023 to December 2026 and is being delivered in partnership with the Nest Center for Journalism Innovation and Development. It draws on the experience of six outlets supported by the International Fund (Graph.mn, iToim, Lemon Press Digital, NTV, UB.life, and Zuunii Medee), setting out what has worked so far, why, and how these lessons might apply to funding public interest media elsewhere.

The early results are striking. In the first 18 months, five of the six grantees increased their non-grant revenue, with a median rise of 23%, compared with 15% across the International Fund’s wider portfolio. This revenue covers, on average, 42% of operating costs. All six improved their operating profit margins, even as costs typically rose by 41% because of new investments. Only three had positive margins at the start, and the cohort median now stands at 32%, against 7% for the wider portfolio. The cohort's workforce also grew by 6%, at a time when many newsrooms worldwide have been shrinking.

These gains came in a challenging environment. Many independent outlets cover their running costs through commercial income, but years of tight margins have left little room to invest in new products, audiences, or technology. Press freedom has also narrowed: Mongolia fell from 68th to 102nd in the Reporters Without Borders (RSF) World Press Freedom Index between 2021 and 2025.

The brief sets out five key insights. The first four explore the factors behind the cohort's performance, and the final one focuses on the enabling conditions that made it possible:

1. Building on solid foundations: flexible funding accelerated growth where the foundations were already in place. Most grantees already ran lean, commercially viable models, so unrestricted funding went into experimentation and strategic investment rather than day-to-day survival. iToim, for example, grew its non-grant revenue by 125% by shifting from one-off contracts to long-term advertising deals with ethical partners.

2. Turning funding into measurable outcomes: diagnostics, planning workshops, monthly check-ins, and performance tracking from FT Strategies and Nest helped outlets set clear, data-driven goals. Grantees cited strategic clarity as one of the programme's main benefits.

3. A trusted local partner: Nest's in-country knowledge shaped the grantee selection, the design of the support package, and legal assistance for outlets facing harassment. This has kept external support closely aligned with the realities of the Mongolian market.

4. Strengthening the wider sector through a cohort: bringing together a diverse group of influential outlets encouraged peer learning, joint reporting, and collective action. This included a coordinated response to a draft Press Freedom Law and shared work on a Mongolian-language AI tool that no single outlet could have built alone.

5. A convergence of favourable conditions: the results reflect commercially capable grantees, a relatively stable media environment, a responsive market with demand for trustworthy journalism, and strong local support. Where organisations face acute financial pressure, the same funding may simply be absorbed into keeping the lights on.

Together, the insights show how flexible funding, combined with strategic and local support, can accelerate the growth of independent media that is already on a sound footing. The findings are not yet final. A fuller picture of the grantees' long-term sustainability will only emerge after the programme ends in December 2026. Still, the Mongolian experience offers a valuable contribution to a pressing question for the sector: what makes funding a catalyst, not a crutch, for independent media?

About the learning brief series

This learning brief is part of a series produced by the International Fund's What Works Unit, which documents and analyses the experience of independent media in low- and middle-income countries to understand what works and what does not in responding to the political and structural market challenges facing public interest journalism.

Growing food has never been easy. Farmers make decisions every day on things they can't completely control: Will the rain come on time? Will temperatures stay manageable? Will pests destroy the crops? Is the soil healthy?

There has always been uncertainty, but climate change is making many of those conditions harder to predict. And for farmers operating on small plots, whose work supports businesses and jobs far beyond the farm, those changes can mean smaller harvests and lower incomes.

For example, in sub-Saharan Africa, where around 80% of food is produced by smallholder farmers, the problem is especially pressing. But why does that matter for the rest of us?

When farming gets harder, the effects don't stop at the farm

Farms are only the beginning of the food system. A harvest of maize, for example, might start on a farm, then might be sold to a distributor, then to a grocery store or market, and eventually make its way to someone's kitchen. In fact, around 70–75% of the price consumers pay for food is created after it leaves the farm.

Multiply that journey by all the food we eat and you start to see what a food system really is: an entire network of people, businesses, processors, sellers, and consumers involved in getting food from farm to plate.

In parts of Africa, about half the population depends on primary agriculture — the process of growing crops and raising animals to produce food and other raw materials--for a living. When you include the wider agrifood system, it accounts for roughly two-thirds of all jobs.

So when a farmer has a difficult season, the consequences can ripple outward. The farmer has less food to sell and less income to spend. A trader has less to buy. A transporter has less product to move. Businesses throughout the local area can feel the effects. A shock to a small farm can be a shock to the entire community.

The reverse is also true: When farms become more productive and reliable, those gains can create more income and opportunity throughout the food system. A farmer who sells more can invest in the next season: better seed, a water pump, improved storage, or an extra pair of hands at harvest. Traders, transporters, and shops have more to buy, move, and sell. And across millions of farms, countries can grow more of the food they need and spend less importing it.

Women are especially important to these systems. In sub-Saharan Africa, 76% of working women are employed in agrifood systems. Yet women farmers can face additional barriers in accessing things like land, technology, financing, information, and markets, all of which can make adapting to changing conditions more difficult.

Ultimately, what happens on farms affects whether communities have reliable access to nutritious food. In 2025, 2.69 billion people — nearly one-third of the world’s population — could not afford a healthy diet.

Farmers are already finding ways to adapt

There isn't one solution to helping farmers with climate adaptation. But new tools are making it possible for farmers to make better decisions, protect their harvests and income, and get more from the resources they already have. Here are three examples making a difference:

Better information about weather

Farmers have always watched the weather. Now, more precise forecasts can give them better information about what's coming.

In Kenya, TomorrowNow and the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) are making hyperlocal weather information available to more than 6 million farmers.

That information can help a farmer answer very practical questions like: Is rain likely this week? When is the right time to plant? Better information doesn't eliminate the risk of a drought or flood. But it can give farmers more time to prepare and protect a season's worth of income.

Crops that can handle tougher conditions

Another approach is developing crops that are better suited to the conditions farmers are experiencing now. Researchers are working with farmers to develop varieties that can better withstand challenges such as drought, heat, pests, and disease.

In Uganda, for example, scientist Dr. Clare Mukankusi at CGIAR, a global research partnership dedicated to a food-secure future, developed new bean varieties to thrive in drier conditions and poorer soil.

For a farmer, a hardier crop can mean the difference between losing most of a harvest and having enough to eat and sell.

Better information about soil

Healthy crops also depend on healthy soil. But farmers can’t always tell what their soil needs simply by looking at it. Soil-mapping tools can provide a clearer picture of what is happening beneath the surface and help farmers make more informed decisions about how to manage their land.

In Kenya, a tool called Virtual Agronomist uses digital soil maps to help farmers understand what their soil needs and make better decisions about fertilizer.

Combined with innovations designed to improve soil health, that information can help farmers use limited resources more effectively and keep their land productive.

A more resilient food system

No technology can make agriculture risk-free. But better forecasts, stronger crops, healthier soils, and other innovations, such as irrigation, can give farmers more options as conditions change.

The goal is simple: help farmers produce food more reliably and earn more from what they produce.

When that happens, the benefits can extend well beyond an individual farm. Families can earn more stable incomes. Local businesses can grow. Communities can have more reliable food supplies. And food systems can become better prepared for whatever comes next.

Growing food is becoming more difficult. But farmers, scientists, governments, and businesses are already finding ways to adapt—and getting those solutions into the hands of more farmers can help build a more resilient future for all of us.

SCDT Executive Director Kia Smith (left) teaching staff members Sabrina Boggs and Jessica Jones-Lewis some moves.

When we decide to fund an organization, we’ve seen that “magic spark” that makes them special — but for board members, who only see the work on paper, it can be hard to grasp. To enhance the vision, our board and staff gathered for a two-day tour at the end of September, visiting several of our Chicago grantees on the South and North sides of the city. Beyond demonstrating the excellence of individual grantees, the tour highlighted the through line of our work: people taking care of people, and how the entire community benefits as a result.

About the Tour

For the first stop on the tour, the team visited South Chicago Dance Theatre (SCDT) in Hyde Park for a special rehearsal of their interactive dance showcase, during which ensemble members performed in different styles and Founder and Creative Director Kia Smith taught us a few dance moves. The rehearsal wrapped up with a Q&A where the dancers discussed their physically demanding lifestyles, the necessity of working multiple jobs as artists, and how SCDT eases the burden with competitive pay and comprehensive health benefits, the latter of which is almost unheard of at other companies.

We then went to Chicago United Solidarity Project‘s (CUSP) Sharehouse in Englewood. CUSP co-stewards Amanda Williams and Jared Honn shared the breadth of their work in mutual aid and community infrastructure, as well as the impact of our fresh food partnership and their plans for future growth. We were able to see firsthand the scale of goods they are distributing across the city through their Sharehouse, from shelf-stable food, to clean drinking water, to diapers and formula.

Left: CUSP’s Sharehouse. Right: CUSP Co-Steward Jared Honn talking to our team.

The first day concluded at Public Media Institute‘s (PMI) building Co-Prosperity, an artist hub and gallery space in Bridgeport. Lumpen Radio Director Stephanie Manriquez walked us through the space, including their risograph printing station and broadcasting station, and explained how PMI’s work sits in the intersection of cultural programming and artist-run mutual aid. Their exhibition at the time, “Between Memory and Becoming: Manifestations of Black Motherhood,” was curated by WILD YAMS, who recently joined the LoganArts cohort. We were honored to sit with the artists, who talked through their art and art-making process.

WILD YAMS artist presenting her work at Co-Prosperity.

The following morning, we visited Sarah’s at Lakeside, one of Sarah’s Circle’s buildings in Uptown that provides 28 fully furnished studio apartments as part of their Permanent Supportive Housing (PSH) program for women experiencing homelessness. The building also provides additional program and communal space, a demonstration kitchen, and administrative offices. We spoke to staff members Lee Poe, Foundations Relations Manager and Kathleen Molnar, LCSW, Director of External Resources about the severe shortage of affordable housing in Chicago, with more than 1,800 unhoused women sleeping on the streets on any given night. Sarah’s Circle is a safe space for these women, welcoming them with safety, respect, and community. 

The last stop was Global Gardens in Albany Park, where Executive Director Haley LeRand led the team through a tour of their one-acre farm. Global Gardens’ mission is to facilitate reconnection with cultural foods and cultivation practices, build community, and promote sustainable growth and equitable food access. Refugee families grow produce from their home countries like opo squash, bitter melon, and sour leaf — a taste of home. Additionally, through their market farmers program, refugee farmers earn income from their harvest at farmers markets, restaurants, and Global Gardens’ CSA program.

Produce grown at Global Gardens.

Feedback From Our Board

Rozina Breen, our board director who traveled all the way from Leeds, England, said: “The privilege of sitting on a board really comes to life when you get to meet the grantees you’re supporting. Of course it’s they who are front and centre of our work; and who teach us so much about the world around us and the values of resilience, courage, community and humanity. It was a humbling, enlivening and inspiring 48 hours which perfectly illustrated the might of movement building and the strength of the collective approach.“

Chicago-based board director Jim Hellige said: “It was greatly rewarding to go on the recent tour of some of the Foundation’s grantees. It was impressive to see the significant impact the Foundation has on smaller, in some case almost “start-up”, nonprofits that have a big impact in the neighborhoods they serve. These capable leaders have chosen a path of service to their communities when they certainly could have found a different kind of success following an alternative path. It is very inspiring.”

Het is zondagavond in Driehuis als de deurbel gaat. Voor de deur staat Winston met zijn gouden koffer. Louis en Sandra hebben Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht niet gekeken. Ze hebben dan ook geen idee welke verrassing hen te wachten staat. 

woensdag 14 oktober 2026 - Winnaarsverhalen

Een avond vol verrassingen

Sandra komt verwonderd de trap af. “Dat meen je niet,” zegt ze. Als Winston de cheque onthult, is de verbazing groot: Louis en Sandra winnen € 370.000,-, hetzelfde bedrag als studiowinnaar Gerda uit Wilp. “Dat wordt een vrije dag morgen,” grapt Louis. 

Samen herinneringen maken

Louis en Sandra hebben een reparatiebedrijf voor scheepsmotoren, twee kinderen en twee kleinkinderen. “Onze kinderen zijn gezond, onze kleinkinderen zijn gezond. Wat wil je nog meer?” zegt Sandra. Hun wens: zoveel mogelijk leuke dingen doen met hun dierbaren. 

Meer winnaars in Driehuis

Het feest in Driehuis is nog niet voorbij! Ook de andere deelnemers op postcode 1985 ER vallen in de prijzen. Zij winnen bedragen van € 19.473,- tot € 58.421,-, afhankelijk van het aantal loten. Omdat Louis en Sandra met meer loten meespelen, winnen zij nog eens € 38.947,- extra.

Kijk je mee?

Tussen 6 september en 18 oktober 2026 geniet je iedere zondag om 19:55 uur van Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht op SBS6. Wil je Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht terugkijken? Dat kan via KIJK.nl.

Dag en nacht staan de vrijwilligers van de Koninklijke Nederlandse Redding Maatschappij (KNRM) klaar. Voor mensen en dieren in nood. Ook op plekken waar andere hulpdiensten moeilijk kunnen komen. Dankzij onze deelnemers ontving de KNRM € 1 miljoen voor 4 nieuwe kusthulpverleningsvoertuigen. Op 10 oktober is het eerste voertuig officieel in gebruik genomen.

woensdag 14 oktober 2026 - Goede doelen

Hulp waar dat hard nodig is

De KNRM gebruikt de voertuigen op het strand, in de duinen en op andere moeilijk bereikbare plekken. Bijvoorbeeld bij zoekacties. Vrijwilligers rijden ermee naar mensen in nood en vervoeren gewonden. Ook kunnen de voertuigen kleinere reddingboten trekken.

Te hulp in de duinen

Hoe belangrijk zo’n voertuig is, bleek op 18 januari 2026. In de Zuidduinen van Noordwijk kwam iemand ten val en raakte gewond aan het onderbeen. Andere hulpdiensten konden de plek moeilijk bereiken. 

Vrijwilligers van de KNRM reden daarom met een kusthulpverleningsvoertuig de duinen in. Ze brachten de gewonde persoon op een brancard uit het gebied. Daarna droegen ze die over aan het ambulancepersoneel. 

Vier nieuwe voertuigen dankzij deelnemers 

“De vrijwilligers van de KNRM staan dag en nacht klaar voor mensen in nood. Daarbij moeten zij kunnen rekenen op moderne en betrouwbare voertuigen die passen bij hun reddingwerk. Dankzij de deelnemers van de Postcode Loterij kan de KNRM 4 van deze voertuigen aanschaffen. Daar zijn we ontzettend dankbaar voor”, vertelt Anneke Salden, relatiebeheerder bij de KNRM. 

Klaar voor de toekomst

De 4 nieuwe voertuigen vervangen oudere voertuigen. Ze zijn speciaal gemaakt voor reddingswerk op verschillende soorten stranden en in duingebieden. 

Ook zijn ze duurzamer. De voertuigen rijden op HVO100, een duurzamer alternatief voor gewone diesel. Daardoor stoten ze tot 90 procent minder CO₂ en fijnstof uit. 

De voertuigen hebben ook moderne hulpmiddelen. Met warmtebeeldcamera’s kunnen vrijwilligers mensen beter zoeken, vooral in het donker. Camera’s rondom het voertuig geven de bestuurder beter zicht tijdens het rijden.

Nonprofits today are navigating challenging and uncertain times — funding cuts, shifting political headwinds, digital and physical security threats, and, in some cases, hard conversations about organizational sustainability. This list gathers free resources, funded in part by the Hewlett Foundation, that are available to any nonprofit looking for support with strategic transitions, legal assistance, financial resilience, digital security, and board governance.

GLOBAL

Access Now provides digital security support for organizations around the world. Reach the team at help@accessnow.org.

Civic Strength Partners helps organizations plan for strategic transitions, mergers and partnerships, restructuring, and protection of assets. Support includes matchmaking, transition preparation support, and merger accompaniment and implementation guidance. Expertise includes legal, governance, finance, strategy, communications, HR, and responsible asset disposition. Reach out here.

PILnet (Global Network of Public Interest Law) offers pro bono access to legal expertise to meet the needs of nonprofits, and to strengthen organizations working for a more just and equitable world. Get legal assistance here.

The Cyrus R. Vance Center for International Justiceengages lawyers globally to support civil society and an ethically active legal profession. It offers legal assistance to organizations working to protect the environment, human rights, institutional integrity and others. Reach out here.

US DOMESTIC

Democracy Protection Networkprovides assistance with physical security, cybersecurity, crisis communications, and legal advice and representation for organizations whose issue areas are impacted by shrinking democratic space. Apply here.

Nonprofit GPShelps nonprofit leaders make well-informed decisions and navigate business model risks to keep their mission alive, even in disruptive times. It draws on the grounded experience of Nonprofit Financial Commons and BDO’s Nonprofit and Grantmaker Advisory practice, as well as the tools at StrongNonprofits.org and other collaborating networks, offering:

  • Publicly available resources
  • Peer convenings and webinars
  • A free, confidential helpline for financial and organizational management

Sign up here to receive their latest updates and resources.

NGO-ISAC helps strengthen the security of nonprofits by bringing them together in a collaborative community where they can share information, learn from one another, and stay ahead of emerging threats to civil society. Nonprofits can join here.

Democracy Notes is a trade publication and field-support organization serving the U.S. democracy space. Its goal is to connect people and share sector-specific information through field news, peer-learning cohorts, events, and research. They recently launched a Wellbeing Resource Library.

Conservation Capacity Project offers free webinars, curated resources, well-being support, and one-on-one coaching and technical assistance to conservation nonprofits and Tribes. To access the free offerings and organizational coaching from experts in areas such as fundraising, communications, digital security, and strategic partnerships, join the mailing list here.

BoardSource

All Hewlett grantees have access to an annual BoardSource membership, which includes hundreds of governance tools and resources, Ask the Expert service, a dedicated community for grantees and board members to connect and collaborate, and a comprehensive on-demand training program. Set up your BoardSource membership by completing this form.

How POCUS is changing pregnancy care in Kenya

At Nasusi Health Centre in Bungoma County, Kenya, Nursing Officer Christine Watima gently pressed her hands against an expectant mother’s abdomen. She felt only a single contour, but her instinct told her that the patient might be carrying twins.

She reached for the clinic’s new point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) device to pair her clinical judgment with a closer look at what was happening with the pregnancy.

Unlike traditional ultrasound machines that are typically housed in larger health facilities, POCUS devices are compact and portable, allowing trained health workers to perform scans where patients are already receiving care.

What the scan revealed

The ultrasound scan confirmed a twin pregnancy—reason enough for the mother to deliver at a higher-level facility—but it also revealed that one of the babies was in a breech position. A breech delivery—bottom- or feet- first rather than head first—has a higher risk of complications. Watima referred the mother to a facility equipped for specialized monitoring and delivery care.

The need for portable, easy-to-use ultrasound

For many pregnant women in rural Kenya, getting that kind of information isn’t simple. Many primary health facilities lack ultrasound equipment, so getting a scan can mean traveling as far as 40 kilometers to a major urban medical center. The high cost of transportation can put scans out of reach altogether.

“It’s estimated that approximately one in 10 pregnant women [in rural Kenya] have access to an ultrasound machine during pregnancy.”

POCUS gives trained health workers like Watima more confidence to act on their experience and knowledge and what they learn from their patients and from physical exams.

With a small probe and an application of gel, the device translates sound waves into real-time images, helping health workers make better-informed referrals when a pregnancy needs a higher level of care.

A different plan for delivery

Months later, Watima’s patient safely delivered two healthy baby boys via a scheduled cesarean section. Today, she remains a regular visitor to the clinic, stopping by to say hello to the nurse she regards as not only a clinician but also a champion who helped ensure the safe birth of her twins.

“Now nurses can help mothers in a way we never could before, with timely referrals”

Strengthening care closer to home

As more primary health facilities in western Kenya gain access to POCUS, health workers are noticing that more women are coming in earlier for prenatal care and staying engaged with their care throughout their pregnancies. Women are even accessing breast cancer screening through POCUS.

“[Women] coming in early for antenatal care and also completing the recommended visits is an early sign that we are in the right direction.”

The partnerships making it possible

A handheld device may be small, but getting it into the hands of a trained health worker takes a much larger partnership. This work is made possible by the Academic Model Providing Access to Healthcare (AMPATH), a partnership in Kenya between Moi University, the public health system, and global academic partners through the AMPATH Consortium. Support for the POCUS initiative is provided through Panorama Global, a U.S. charitable foundation, with funding from the Gates Foundation, Novartis, Eli Lilly and Company, and MSD, through its MSD for Mothers initiative.

“The aim is to deliver quality health care in underserved communities [and] to train health care workers for this and the next generation,” says Dr. Laktabai.

Through care, education, and research, AMPATH ensures that health workers are not isolated in their practice and that mothers can access high-quality prenatal care without the burden and expense of traveling long distances. By July 2026, more than 60% of facilities across three Kenyan counties had POCUS devices.

7,000

That means more women are getting the right care at the right time—and more local health workers are able to make clinical decisions with confidence and offer patients greater reassurance and hope.

Marijke staat op het punt om met haar zoontje te verhuizen. Tussen alle verhuisdozen door krijgt ze onverwacht bezoek van Winston. En hij komt niet met lege handen. Marijke wint maar liefst € 145.000,-. Marijke wint als thuiswinnaar hetzelfde bedrag als studiowinnaar Bert uit Zutphen, in de 5e aflevering van Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht. 

woensdag 7 oktober 2026 - Winnaarsverhalen

Druk met de verhuizing

Marijke woont samen met haar zoontje in Haaften. Binnenkort verhuizen ze naar een nieuwe plek, iets verderop in het dorp. Daarom staat haar huis nu vol met spullen en verhuisdozen. Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht heeft ze die avond niet gezien. “Ik kijk soms, maar nu was ik druk met inpakken”, vertelt ze. Marijke heeft dus geen idee welk bedrag er die avond is gewonnen.

Een wens voor het nieuwe huis

Als Winston vraagt of ze nog wensen heeft voor haar nieuwe huis, hoeft Marijke niet lang na te denken. Ze wil graag een mooie visgraatvloer. “Nou, die gaat er komen!”, zegt Winston en schrijft het gewonnen bedrag op de koffer. Marijke kijkt vol verbazing naar het bedrag. “Wauw, ik ben er sprakeloos van.” 

Buurt wint mee

Een kennis van Marijke won eerder de PostcodeKanjer in Tiel. Dat inspireerde haar om ook mee te spelen. Nu wint ze zelf. En haar buurt wint mee: deelnemers op postcode 4175 CV ontvangen € 14.500,- tot € 29.000,-, afhankelijk van het aantal loten. 

Kijk je mee?

Tussen 6 september en 18 oktober 2026 geniet je iedere zondag om 19:55 uur van Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht op SBS6. Wil je Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht terugkijken? Dat kan via KIJK.nl.

Across 2024 and 2025, Moldova held a series of pivotal elections: a presidential election, a referendum on EU accession, and parliamentary elections. Each unfolded under intense foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI), increasingly channelled through local voices. Our new learning brief Independent media and democratic resilience — the second in our Moldova series — builds on the first to draw out the lessons learned by independent media across this period. Drawing on the experience of ten outlets supported by the International Fund (Agora, Diez, Jurnal TV, Newsmaker, Nokta, SP, Studio-L, TV8, TV Nord, and Ziarul de Gardă), alongside interviews with key figures in the political and media landscape, the learning brief sets out concrete examples of how the country's independent media responded, what worked, and how their learnings might translate across other settings. 

The stakes, and the role independent media played, were summed up by Natalia Gavriliță, former prime minister of Moldova and now an IFPIM board member:  “Our country resisted, and continues to resist, because it applied the so-called whole-of-society approach, in which practically all institutions worked in tandem and complemented one another in countering FIMI while independent media was probably one of the most important elements in this equation.”

That contribution came in a fast-changing information environment. Social media is now a primary source of news for around 80% of Moldovans, though television remains the most trusted. Audiences are also split along linguistic lines, with Romanian- and Russian-speaking communities relying on different platforms and sources — a divide that shaped both where disinformation spread and how independent media had to work to reach people.

The brief sets out six key insights. The first four explore effective strategies used by independent media and the final two focus on key enabling conditions that supported their impact:

1. Leading the conversation, not just countering falsehoods: Independent media were most effective when they reported on complex geopolitical issues through the lens of their audiences' everyday concerns, addressing the anxieties that manipulation sought to exploit rather than only debunking claims.

2. Understanding audiences and platforms: Reach and engagement grew where outlets understood how audiences actually consume information, adapting their formats and distribution accordingly.

3. Exposing the machinery of disinformation: Investigative reporting played a distinct role, revealing the networks and systems behind interference.

4. Amplifying through collaboration: Increasingly, outlets built on one another's work, so that public-interest journalism travelled further across the sector than any single outlet could achieve alone.

5. Supporting a diverse ecosystem: National, regional, and minority-language outlets played complementary and impactful roles, reaching diverse communities and language groups. 

6. Providing flexible core funding: Stable, unrestricted support gave outlets the editorial freedom to retain staff, sustain investigations, experiment with new formats, and respond to fast-moving threats as they emerged.

Together, the insights highlight how the strength and diversity of the ecosystem as a whole enabled independent media to meaningfully counter foreign interference and maximise their impact. 

‍‍

This learning brief is part of a series produced by The International Fund's What Works Unit, which documents and analyses the experience of independent media in low- and middle-income countries to understand what works and what doesn't in responding to the political and structural market challenges facing public interest journalism.

Een zwembad in de tuin

Samen eten is zoveel meer dan een maaltijd. Even bijpraten met je buurvrouw. Lachen met vrienden. Of eindelijk weer eens uitgebreid horen hoe het met je familie gaat. Aan tafel ontstaat vanzelf ruimte voor elkaar.

maandag 5 oktober 2026 - Goede doelen

Drukke agenda’s

Toch schiet samen eten er best vaak bij in. Bijna de helft van de Nederlanders zegt dat het er regelmatig niet van komt. We zijn druk, agenda’s lopen door elkaar en voor je het weet eet je toch alleen of met je eigen gezin. Dat blijkt uit onderzoek van Motivaction onder 1.025 Nederlanders.

Meer behoefte aan samen eten

Terwijl we juist graag wat vaker samen aan tafel zitten. Meer dan een derde van de Nederlanders wil vaker eten met mensen buiten het eigen huishouden. En driekwart vindt dat samen eten mensen dichter bij elkaar brengt.

Een klein gebaar, een gezellig moment

Het goede nieuws? Het hoeft helemaal niet ingewikkeld te zijn. Voor 80% van de Nederlanders hoeft een gezamenlijke maaltijd niet uitgebreid of perfect te zijn. Veel belangrijker zijn gezelligheid, aandacht voor elkaar en je welkom voele

Schuif lekker aan

Dus schuif die stoelen maar aan. Nodig je buren, familie of vrienden uit. Zet iets lekkers op tafel en maak er samen een fijn moment van. Om je op weg te helpen, ontvangt elke deelnemer een Schuif lekker aan cadeaukaart t.w.v. € 15,-. Daarmee haal je bij Albert Heijn boodschappen voor een lekkere maaltijd samen. Want soms is één uitnodiging alles wat nodig is.

En samen doen we nóg meer

In deze periode zijn 2 Schuif lekker aan verspakketten gekoppeld aan Resto VanHarte. Voor ieder verkocht pakket doneren Albert Heijn en de Postcode Loterij € 0,50 aan deze organisatie. Resto VanHarte brengt mensen samen tijdens betaalbare diners en lunches. Zo ontstaan nieuwe ontmoetingen en helpt de organisatie eenzaamheid tegen te gaan. 

Dus: wie nodig jij binnenkort uit om lekker aan te schuiven?

De zon breekt net door als Quinty Rijswijk binnenrijdt. Ze heeft bijzonder nieuws bij zich. 11 deelnemers met postcode 2286 NA verdelen samen € 500.000,-. Voor de winnaars begint een middag vol verrassingen, dromen en mooie plannen.

vrijdag 2 oktober 2026 - Winnaarsverhalen

De grote prijs

Malina en John zijn als eerste aan de beurt. Ze weten nog niet wat hen te wachten staat. Even later hebben ze een cheque van maar liefst € 250.000,- in handen. Wat ze met het geld gaan doen? Ze willen hun serre en badkamer verbouwen. En er staat nog een bijzondere wens op hun lijstje: een reis naar Suriname. 

Nog meer winnaars

Maar het mooiste vinden ze dat het feest niet bij hun voordeur stopt. “Het is nog leuker om samen met de buren te winnen”, vertellen ze. En dat gebeurt. De andere € 250.000,- wordt verdeeld onder deelnemers die met dezelfde postcode meespelen. 

Een bijzondere lunchpauze

Ook Derk krijgt onverwacht bezoek. Hij is gewoon aan het werk als het team voor zijn deur staat. Met een cheque in zijn handen kan hij een grap niet laten: “Ik heb nog nooit zoveel verdiend in mijn lunchpauze.” De timing had bijna niet mooier gekund. De volgende dag vieren Derk en zijn partner hun 25-jarig huwelijk. “Dus dit komt heel goed van pas!” 

Dromen van verre reizen

Terwijl de cheques worden uitgereikt, komen ook de eerste dromen boven tafel. Bij verschillende winnaars gaat het gesprek al snel over reizen. Sanneke wil met haar gezin “op een heel mooie vakantie met z’n vieren”. Ook Monique kijkt verder dan de landsgrenzen. “Ik wil graag een reis buiten Europa maken.”

Den 1 oktober tar Postkodlotteriets Stiftelse nästa steg i sin utveckling genom att lansera en ny visuell identitet och logotyp.

För de flesta kommer förändringen att märkas främst genom nya färger, uppdaterad formgivning och en ny logotyp i våra kanaler. Men bakom förändringen finns ett större gemensamt arbete som omfattar samtliga stiftelser inom Postcode Lottery Group och går i linje med lotteriernas nya logotyp och visuella uttryck. 

Den nya logotypen kommer successivt att införas på vår webbplats, i sociala medier, i våra publikationer och i annat material som vi producerar.

Det är viktigt att understryka att förändringen handlar om hur vi ser ut, inte om vilka vi är. Vårt uppdrag, vårt arbete och vårt engagemang för att stötta organisationer och initiativ som bidrar till ett bättre samhälle är detsamma som tidigare. Vi är fortfarande samma stiftelse, men i en ny kostym.

För organisationer och projekt som har ett pågående samarbete med oss kommer den nya identiteten inte att innebära några förändringar i våra processer eller i det stöd som ges. Berörda projekt kommer att få mer information om vad förändringen innebär och hur den kan påverka användningen av våra logotyper och annat kommunikationsmaterial.

Vi ser fram emot att introducera vår nya visuella identitet och fortsätta arbetet tillsammans med Postkodlotteriet, våra partners, projekt och organisationer.

Den nya visuella identiteten lanseras den 1 oktober 2026. Vi hoppas att ni kommer att uppskatta den lika mycket som vi gör.
