Bringing together paleoclimatologists, geologists, and astrophysicists, The CycloAstro Project supports collaboration across disciplines to investigate the history of the solar system by looking directly through Earth’s geological record. As part of its grantmaking toward research that provides the scientific foundation for understanding climate change and its effects on our planet and humankind, the Heising-Simons Foundation’s Science program has been supporting the project’s first and second phases at various institutions through $9 million in grants, prioritizing diverse perspectives to feed scientific breakthroughs.

Read the full story below.

Reading the Solar System in Earth’s Geological Record

“[CycloAstro] brings together scientists with a huge range of expertise, challenging us to continuously step back from our respective corners of the puzzle and look at the bigger picture.”

Malena Rice, Ph.D., 51 pegasi b alumna and Yale University astronomy professor

Dr. Malena Rice’s science career began with a simple dream: to personally save the world. Naturally, she went into pre-med. What better way to save the world than to save lives, right? Well, the universe had other plans. Rice—still an undergrad student—took an astronomy class and was convinced to pursue the field. She made herself a promise then: to study the stars until they weren’t fun anymore.

“That continues to be my perspective,” she says. “Astronomy remains a delight.”

Today, Dr. Rice, a 51 Pegasi b alumna, is an astronomy professor at Yale University, where she completed her Ph.D. She recounts her early motivations from her office desk. Behind her, a black chalkboard is covered in scribbles, equations, and calculations. “I like brainstorming on the chalkboard,” she laughs. Some of what’s there are the remnants of one of her major research collaborations: The CycloAstro Project.

The CycloAstro Project is unlike any other scientific endeavor to understand the physical world—and that’s because its scientists are trying to investigate the history of the solar system by looking directly through Earth’s geological record. Inside each ice cap and beneath every lake, miles of ice, sediment, and mud tell a roughly 4-billion-year-old story of how our planet and solar system formed. The group is analyzing these data to extend astronomical models beyond their current time limit: 50 million years ago. The team has succeeded in probing the geological record to model our solar system evolution, including the tilt and orbit shape variations of every planet and the Earth-Moon system. To accomplish all this, the team has brought together more than 30 experts from a variety of disciplines, including paleoclimatology, geology, and astrophysics.

The group is diverse in more ways than one. There is their varied expertise, of course, but the researchers also represent multiple nationalities, genders, socioeconomic backgrounds, religions, and more. This element is key to CycloAstro’s success and pizazz. It’s also a fundamental characteristic that the Heising-Simons Foundation nurtures as CycloAstro’s sole funder since its inception in 2021. The project’s second phase, CycloAstro2.0, will run through 2031 at various institutions with $4 million in grants from the foundation.

“It’s so incredibly special,” Dr. Rice says. “The project brings together scientists with a huge range of expertise, challenging us to continuously step back from our respective corners of the puzzle and look at the bigger picture.”

Preliminary research image from a project charting how a potentially hidden and massive Planet Nine in the distant solar system could perturb Earth’s orbit depending on its orbital properties. The existence of Planet Nine could help solve major mysteries about how our solar system formed and how gravity works on a grand scale. Credit: Adamski & Rice.

CycloAstro researchers developed TRACE, or Time-Reversible Algorithm for Close Encounters, a novel open-source algorithm that simulates close encounters between massive bodies. TRACE significantly improves both speed and accuracy over previous state-of-the-art methods, and it’s freely available to other scientists. Credit: Lu, Hernandez & Rein, MNRAS. 

Breaking Down Walls, Creating Opportunities

"What can we do to open doors and reduce the biases we know are prevalent?"

Rocío P​aola Caballero-Gill, Ph.D., Assistant Research Professor, George Mason University

Dr. Rice joined the group two years ago and still hasn’t met most of her colleagues in person, but she feels right at home. The project achieves the rare feat of breaking down the walls between disciplines so everyone can take part, regardless of expertise. For instance, Dr. Rice is the only one focused on exoplanets (these days, she’s questioning whether a Planet Nine could be lurking in the outer solar system), but her coworkers still invite her to engage in rigorous debate and conversation about their subjects. She has contributed to discussions about how the evolving spins of planets in both the solar system and exoplanet systems may be informed by the Earth’s past and present climate dynamics.

“Because we don’t speak the same professional language, it’s easier for me to say something that might sound ridiculous to a geophysicist,” Dr. Rice says. “I’m used to the language of astronomers.”

Yet that vulnerability and openness are exactly what strengthen the science. These qualities didn’t emerge on their own, however. They required intention and cultivation.

At CycloAstro, Dr. Rocío Paola Caballero-Gill curates that culture. A geologist by training, she directs researchers’ relationship-building through CycloAstro’s cohort program. “I support the people who make science possible,” she says. That means she’s the brains behind CycloAstro’s recruitment strategy and team member support, helping the team foster meaningful connections.

Traditionally, scientists gain opportunities based on their connections, Ivy League degrees, and prolific publishing. Dr. Caballero-Gill co-designed CycloAstro’s approach with her team to find talent they may otherwise miss. This included open office hours to offer mentorship and guidance to anyone interested in joining. During the application process, CVs are not required. Instead, applicants must answer a few questions about how their skills align with the project goals. The group also asked references to answer a questionnaire to gauge whether the applicant’s skill set fits their needs, rather than requesting a typical letter. This hiring system has since been adopted by a few other organizations, including the Geological Society of America’s On To the Future program and the National Science Foundation’s Code to Communicate.

“What can we do to open doors and reduce the biases we know are prevalent?” she says.

Investing in the people behind the science is Dr. Caballero-Gill’s passion. As a Peruvian woman with a chronic illness who lives in a biracial, multi-generational household, this work is personal. It’s also ongoing. The work doesn’t end once someone’s hired. She regularly checks in with the team to ensure their personal values and long-term career goals align, and finds ways to build mentorship within the group.

2022 cohort at the first in-person CycloAstro gathering in Fairfax, Virginia.

CycloAstro is fostering groundbreaking science, but it’s also paving a different way to do science, where the experts are encouraged to bring their full selves to work. Whether that’s their disability, gender, or caregiver status, the team embraces each other for who they are outside their scientist hats.

“Diversity is essential,” Dr. Caballero-Gill says. “If we are trying to improve the world, the people who make up that world need to be involved as part of the process. Different experiences, particularly those from marginalized communities, don’t just make science more inclusive; they make it better.”

Different Origins, Same Destination

“Looking back, the whole process was a gift. I was blessed by a hell of a lot of luck.”

Paul Olsen, Ph.D., professor at Columbia University’s Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory

Dr. Linda Hinnov, a geology professor at George Mason University, coordinates The CycloAstro Project, finding ways to support everyone’s interests and collaborative efforts. “Everyone is extremely inspiring,” she says. She doesn’t say it, but so is she.

Her father was a physicist, so she grew up overhearing scientific conversations between him and his colleagues. Early on, she developed a curiosity about the underground world of microscopic fossils—foraminifera, to be exact—but her heart was in music. She studied music theory as an undergraduate at Princeton University. However, after taking her university’s science requirement, Dr. Hinnov rediscovered that wonder about the fossil world. She hasn’t looked back since.

It took her years to return to earth science. Her first job involved offshore oil exploration. Eventually, she pursued a master’s in geophysics. During her Ph.D., she realized she could study sedimentary records to examine how changes in Earth’s orbit affected ancient climates. Now, that’s exactly what CycloAstro is doing.

Hinnov sees great value in learning more about the evolution of these planetary dynamics. Paleoclimate change at thousand-to-million-year timescales is influenced by the motions of all the other planets in our solar system, plus the Moon. To understand ancient climate change, scientists need multiple models of Earth’s rotational history, the Earth-Moon system, and solar system planetary dynamics.

“This gives us an opportunity to ground truth all of the models,” Dr. Hinnov says.

Dr. Paul Olsen is one of the paleoastronomers helping collect and assess data that feeds those models. Like Dr. Hinnov, Dr. Olsen didn’t always imagine he’d be studying the stars. He’s now a professor at Columbia University’s Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, but his journey there was full of obstacles.

CycloAstro research demonstrates how geological data from ancient lake sediment cores can be analyzed using automation and AI to reconstruct the historical orbits and planetary frequencies of the Solar System during the Triassic and Jurassic periods (200 to 240 million years ago). Source: Paul E. Olsen, Arthur D. Storke Memorial Professor of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Columbia University, New York.

A famous geological outcrop of the Late Triassic Lockatong Formation located in a quarry in Eureka, Pennsylvania. It functions as a visual diagram demonstrating how ancient climate cycles are recorded vertically in layers of lake sediment (lacustrine cycles). ource: Paul E. Olsen, Arthur D. Storke Memorial Professor of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Columbia University, New York.

His father, a Danish immigrant, had only a third-grade education, and his mother hailed from a coal-mining family. Dr. Olsen grew up wearing an eye patch because of amblyopia. He’s legally blind in his left eye. That didn’t stop him from becoming an artist, though. He even won a few awards for his paintings, but he went the science route. Olsen was an amateur fossil hunter, spending much of his youth searching for dinosaur footprints with his friends. Life even wrote a feature about them in 1970.

That work, Olsen believes, landed him a spot in Yale’s high-risk student program, which was meant to increase diversity at the university. Unfortunately, Dr. Olsen did not excel at math, which geology requires. When calculators and computers came around, Dr. Olsen finally had the tools to succeed. He didn’t let his many challenges stop him from pursuing his dreams. Not when his parents could no longer afford his tuition. Not when he had to sell scientific illustrations to cover school on his own. Not when his program required he take a last-minute German class to satisfy his degree requirements.

Now, Dr. Olsen gets paid to explore data from hundreds of millions of years ago.

“Looking back, the whole process was a gift,” Dr. Olsen says. “I was blessed by a hell of a lot of luck.”

But luck didn’t bring Dr. Olsen or anyone else to CycloAstro. Fate, maybe, but the real force is the people themselves—and their ability to overcome all the hurdles they’ve encountered to get here. Look at Dr. Rice, who studies exoplanets. Her mom came to the U.S. after escaping the Vietnam War by a boat that nearly sank. “She, her family, and so many others lost everything that they had,” Dr. Rice explains. Growing up, her family’s survival felt like a gift—a gift she couldn’t squander.

“I needed to give back to this world where so much was given to me,” she says.

Science Without Silos

"Research like this is non-traditional and is often hard to fund because it doesn't fit cleanly into any single silo—which is exactly what makes it a good fit for philanthropic support."

John O'Brien, Ph.D., Science Program Officer, Heising-Simons Foundation

And that, in a nutshell, is the beauty of CycloAstro. They’re offering a new way of doing science, one that prioritizes collaboration and diverse perspectives to feed breakthroughs. They’re using chemical records from sedimentary cores to map and predict where groundwater may be contaminated, working directly with the Navajo Nation. By modeling solar system evolution, they uncover the cosmic forces that shaped Earth’s climate and environmental history. The project’s research highlights page showcases how science from five research collaborations comes together to trace Solar System evolution, Earth-Moon dynamics, and Earth’s paleoclimate system with state-of-the-art analysis and modeling. CycloAstro’s collaborative culture was enriched by the contributions of phase 1 scholars: Steve Meyers, Alberto Malinverno, Lorraine Lisiecki, Sean Kinney, Richard Zeebe, Greg Laughlin, Margriet Lantink, Ridwan Ajibade, Jonathan Hammer, Yuxin Zhou, Yujing Wu, David Hernandez, Ilja Kocken, Daniel Seggesseman, Carmen McCallum, and Julie Libarkin, amongst others.

John O’Brien, Ph.D., Program Officer at the Heising-Simons Foundation, emphasizes, “The CycloAstro collaboration is a wonderful example of a group of scientists with diverse but related interests coming together to build a truly unique research program that brings together knowledge from a multitude of scientific disciplines. Research like this is non-traditional and is often hard to fund because it doesn’t fit cleanly into any single silo—which is exactly what makes it a good fit for philanthropic support.”

This story was written by Yessenia Funes. She is available on all major social media @yessfun.

On October 30th at the Barbican Centre in London, investigative journalists and allies from around the world will gather for “Overreach,” the 6th biennial CIJ Logan Symposium. We recently had the pleasure to interview James Harkin, Executive Director of The Centre of Investigative Journalism and board director of the Reva and David Logan Foundation, about the conference.

Can you explain the origin of the CIJ Logan Symposium and how it has since evolved?
The CIJ Logan Symposium dates back to 2014. It was originally established because something new and exciting was happening in the world of investigative journalism. Partly because of technology and partly because of politics, investigative journalism was rapidly changing and new people were using technology to facilitate leaks and to help whistleblowers, most notably in the case of WikiLeaks’ early work on Afghanistan. 

As a result of that, Richard Logan and Gavin MacFadyen, the founder-director of CIJ, came together to create a journalism conference that not only speaks to journalists but to their new allies within this brave new world. It thinks about how best to protect those new allies—be they sources, whistleblowers, slightly crazy hackers—and beyond that, it thinks critically about what investigative journalism has been, what it is, and what it’s becoming.

What I love about the symposium is that it’s much less self-congratulatory than similar journalism conferences. Often you will see echo chambers of journalists who all say the same things. That can be kind of boring after a while. Our symposium is rather different from that—it brings everyone together to think outside the box, in an avant garde way, about how to make investigative journalism better. 

In terms of how it’s evolved, the political terrain and technology have changed rapidly. In many ways, the world of investigative journalism is much more fragmented now. But we more or less do the same things: we say what doesn’t get said in other conferences; we defend the kind of people who are slightly beyond the pale; and we are a little bit pricklier and more critical about what’s happening to investigative journalism.

What is most exciting to you about this year’s symposium?
Last time, we tried to think of four interesting but very small nonprofit outlets around the world who were doing amazing stuff. This year, we’ve decided to go a bit more mainstream, but mix that up with more distinctive ideas. 

I honestly believe that this year’s symposium will be the best I’ve ever seen and you will find it nowhere else in the world. Because we stay close to our original mission to speak beyond the echo chamber, we’re capable of getting the best journalists on earth as well as people you’ve never heard of, with ideas that are super interesting and not discussed at any other journalism conference. 

If you want to get a flavor of those speakers, we’ve invited Khadeeja Safdar, who I met first at the Logan Symposium in Berkeley. She is the woman who did that great investigation for the Wall Street Journal about the birthday note Trump sent to Jeffery Epstein. We also invited Hannah Natanson from the Washington Post whose home was searched by the FBI in an attempt to intimidate her and her sources. We have an interesting debate on journalism in Hungary with unusually different opinions, and our opening panel is about the legal assault on investigative journalism. 

We have great names for our panels. We’re doing a panel about the private intelligence agency which is called “Spies Like Us.” Hannah Natanson’s panel is called “Knock Knock.” We’re good at this! Gotta be fun. 

Who is most likely to benefit from the program? What is the importance of bringing together a diverse set of attendees?
In keeping with our mission to broaden investigative journalism and to find new allies, it’s of interest not only to early- and mid-career journalists but to anyone who wants to think critically about the world, who wonders what is happening to journalists, and who wants to learn what is fresh, new and most interesting in terms of tools in the journalism world. 

It’s not an invite-only event. It’s available to anyone who wants to come. We hope that it will appeal to a broad range of people—certainly people from NGOs, the human rights world, politicals. This is extraordinarily good value to get to hang out in the coolest arts venue in the center of London while listening to amazing speakers.

And if we’re thinking about solidarity, a good place for that to start is over a coffee, over a drink, over a free hot lunch.

Het klinkt als een heerlijke, rustige zondag. ’s Middags fietsen Harmannus en Eijka samen een stukje. Daarna gaat de tv aan voor voetbal en wielrennen. Ze weten dan nog niet dat hun zondag een heel andere wending krijgt. Plotseling gaat de deurbel. Als ze opendoen, staat Winston voor de deur. Mét een gouden koffer.

dinsdag 29 september 2026 - Winnaarsverhalen

Heel gelukkig samen

Wanneer Winston de bloemen overhandigt, reageert Eijka enthousiast: “Daar zijn we al blij mee!” Hij vraagt of ze nog wensen hebben. “Om eerlijk te zijn niet”, zegt Eijka. Het stel is heel gelukkig samen in Delfzijl.

De grote onthulling

Dan komt de gouden koffer tevoorschijn. Zodra Winston het gewonnen bedrag onthult, kunnen Eijka en Harmannus hun ogen nauwelijks geloven. “Dat meen je niet! Ongelooflijk, hartstikke mooi”, reageren ze blij.

Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht

Harmannus en Eijka uit Delfzijl zijn de thuiswinnaars van de 4e aflevering van Miljoenenjacht. Ze winnen hetzelfde bedrag als studiowinnaar Jacob uit Westerbroek: € 109.000,-. Ook hun buren die meespelen op postcode 9932 HX winnen mee. Zij verdelen samen ook € 109.000,-. Afhankelijk van het aantal loten waarmee ze meespelen, winnen zij bedragen van € 4.739,- tot € 14.217,-. 

Kijk je mee?

Tussen 6 september en 18 oktober 2026 geniet je iedere zondag om 19:55 uur van Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht op SBS6. Wil je Miljoenenjacht terugkijken? Dat kan via KIJK.nl.

Paris, 25 September: Ahead of World News Day on 28 September, the Forum on Information and Democracy (FID), in partnership with the International Fund for Public Interest Media (IFPIM), has released a short video renewing the call for governments and policymakers to invest in public interest media.

One year ago, the High-Level Panel on Public Interest Media, which was convened by FID and comprising 11 leading economists, published a landmark statement making the economic case for such investment. The statement was picked up by over 80 media outlets and helped shape World News Day's call to action.

Twelve months on, the situation has not improved. Financial pressure on newsrooms continues to intensify, while the rapid growth of AI is reshaping the information ecosystem faster than public interest safeguards can keep pace. Google's AI Overviews are reducing referral traffic to news publishers, and the introduction of advertising within AI chatbots threatens to divert further revenue away from journalism. Meanwhile, the cost of inaction is measurable: disinformation is estimated to cost the global economy $417 billion a year, with Russia alone spending an estimated $1.85 billion annually on foreign propaganda.

Drawing on the High-Level Panel's statement and the recent Value of Journalism report published by the International Fund, UNESCO and DW Akademie, the video presents this evidence in a concise, accessible format. It is a call to action directed at governments and policymakers, and is intended to raise awareness among a wider public.

The video is available with subtitles in English, French, Portuguese and Spanish, alongside a vertical version for social platforms.

In 2024, Kelefors Education Partners evaluated the Foundation’s investments in early math and produced a report highlighting key findings and considerations. In July, The Bridgespan Group published a case study on how funders can measure progress when they invest in building a field to drive systems change. The study draws on Kelefors Education Partners’ 2024 evaluation of the Foundation’s early math investments.

In this Q&A, Kimberly Brenneman, Ph.D., Education Program Officer overseeing the Early Math grantmaking at the Heising-Simons Foundation, discusses the case study’s recommendations for funders aiming to drive systems-level change.

The Bridgespan case study builds upon an external evaluation of the Foundation’s math giving — can you tell us more about that assessment?

Let’s start at the beginning: In 2011, the Heising-Simons Foundation’s Education program launched a comprehensive initiative to improve math learning for children from birth through age 8. Guided by research linking early math proficiency to later academic success, we invested $107 million between 2011 and 2023. The decade-long initiative consisted of three core strategies: advancing early math research, supporting early learning providers—particularly in California—in adopting evidence-based practices, and empowering families to encourage math learning at home. The overarching goal was to ensure that more children have access to effective, enjoyable math opportunities in both educational and community settings. In 2024, we partnered with Kelefors Education Partners to evaluate the impact of a decade of investment. We wanted to understand what has changed in the field of early math over the years we’ve invested and the role our grantmaking played in those changes.

To understand what has changed in the field of early math, Kelefors based their evaluation on Bridgespan’s description of the multiple, observable dimensions of a “field,” including diverse actors and a shared field-level agenda. Kelefors designed measures to assess the extent of positive change across these dimensions since 2011. After Kelefors delivered the evaluation and made a summary public, Bridgespan drew on it to create a case study that shows how a field-building framework can assess philanthropic impact and field-building progress. While early math is the main case presented, other examples from philanthropy support the broader argument. The Bridgespan piece serves as a practical guide for philanthropic organizations interested in field-building and achieving scaled impact. It offers ten recommendations for funders who wish to undertake and evaluate field-building efforts.

What challenges did the Heising-Simons Foundation face regarding measurement, and what did you do differently when taking a field-building approach to grantmaking?

Systemic change and field building often take decades or even a generation to yield population-level results, so the Foundation had to take a long-term view and carefully consider how to measure progress along the way, adjusting its grantmaking strategies as needed. Unlike individual grants or specific lines of work that can often demonstrate quick, quantifiable outcomes, field-building efforts are not easily measured by traditional evaluation tools, which typically focus on discrete outcomes and clear attribution.

Instead of simply asking, “Did we solve this?”, the Foundation shifted its focus to whether it was helping build the conditions for many actors to solve complex problems together. This new approach required building and maintaining collaborative partnerships over time and being prepared to navigate challenges and setbacks as part of the process.

How did the early math field change over the decade of the Foundation’s investment?

The evaluation revealed significant progress in the early math field’s infrastructure and knowledge base between 2011 and 2023, even though ultimate population-level metrics, such as standardized student math scores, remained largely unchanged. For example, the number of early math research articles published in prominent early childhood journals expanded sixfold, from 50 articles before 2012 to 304 articles between 2018 and 2022.

Another exciting finding points to the success of our efforts to find new champions for early math among organizations and individuals already influential in fields like math education, family engagement, or early learning. Among grantees surveyed, 76% said their work shifted in the past decade to include early math, meaning we have many more people and organizations dedicated to spreading opportunities for effective, joyful early math learning by translating the growing knowledge base into tangible action in classrooms and communities.

Additionally, 79% of surveyed education grantees agreed that early math has become a higher priority in educational research, and 59% observed that it is now a higher public policy priority than a decade ago. Funding also helped create highly interconnected, multi-institutional networks, such as the Development and Research in Early Math Education (DREME) network at Stanford University and the Center for Family Math at the National Association of Family, School, and Community Engagement.

What are the top takeaways for other systems-change funders?

Bridgespan’s piece offers 10 core tips for measurement, evaluation, and learning, with a strong emphasis on key operational shifts. One important recommendation is to begin with a baseline field assessment, which provides more objective evidence of change than retrospective assessments that rely on individuals accurately recalling past field conditions. Bridgespan also notes that metrics and scorecards are most valuable when organizations and leaders use them as learning tools, rather than as rigid reporting requirements for funders.

Additionally, the case study underscores that moving population-level indicators, such as statewide or national math proficiency, requires a collective, generational effort—meaning no single foundation can realistically expect to make this progress alone or claim sole credit. Ultimately, Bridgespan concludes that a funder’s true impact often stems from its role as a convener: bringing together peer funders, sharing the risks of experimentation, and building infrastructure that enables hundreds of independent actors to scale solutions over time.

Een gewone zondagavond verandert ineens in een avond om nooit te vergeten. José en Ben uit Sassenheim zitten thuis als er wordt aangebeld. Voor de deur staat Winston. Met bloemen én een gouden koffer. Ze winnen hetzelfde bedrag dat de studiowinnaar in Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht heeft gewonnen.

woensdag 23 september 2026 - Winnaarsverhalen

Het besef moet nog landen 

“Ik zie licht branden, dat is een goed teken”, zegt Winston als hij voor hun huis staat. Hij moet een paar keer aanbellen. Dan gaat de deur open. José en Ben hebben net Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht gekeken. Ze weten dat studiowinnaar Sjoerd uit Lent € 160.000,- heeft gewonnen. Maar dat zij als thuiswinnaars precies hetzelfde bedrag krijgen? Dat moet nog even landen. “Ongelooflijk”, zegt Ben. 

Samen mooie herinneringen maken 

Zodra ze de cheque zien, verschijnt er een brede lach. Na een periode met gezondheidsproblemen kijken ze positief naar de toekomst. En plannen zijn er zeker. “We reizen best wel graag”, vertelt José. Ook hun kinderen en kleinkinderen delen straks in de feestvreugde: ze gaan er samen een mooi feest van maken. 

Meer winnaars in Sassenheim 

Ook de andere deelnemers die meespelen op 2172 DE vallen in de prijzen. Zij verdelen ook nog eens € 160.000,- en winnen bedragen van € 5.333,- tot € 21.333,-, afhankelijk van het aantal loten waarmee iemand meespeelt. José en Ben spelen met meerdere loten mee en winnen daarnaast nog € 16.000,-

Goed nieuws in Alphen aan den Rijn! 5 deelnemers die meespelen op postcode 2406 JT winnen de PostcodeStraatprijs. Dat betekent € 25.000,- per lot en een gloednieuwe BMW voor één van de deelnemers. 

dinsdag 22 september 2026 - Winnaarsverhalen

Een emotioneel moment

Myranda en Rinus wonen in een prachtig huis aan het water, dat ze helemaal zelf hebben opgebouwd. Zodra ze de cheque zien, reageren ze dolblij. “Jeetje joh! Nou, dat is niet verkeerd.” zegt Rinus. Myranda wordt emotioneel en omhelst Gaston. Na een zware periode komt dit mooie nieuws als een fijne meevaller.

De prijs delen

Nicolette en David ontvangen hun cheque in hun tuin, dat grenst aan het water. Ook zij winnen € 25.000,-. Ze delen hun prijs graag met hun 2 kinderen. “Onze jongste wil graag zijn rijbewijs halen en de oudste woont net op zichzelf. Dus dit komt heel goed uit.”

Loch Duart, a Vision Ridge investment, is a small-scale, independent Scottish salmon farming company. Loch Duart produces premium branded salmon with a focus on low-density farming, natural and sustainable feed sourcing, and husbandry. Vision Ridge focuses on environmental sustainability by acquiring inefficiently managed sustainable real assets or converting real assets to more sustainable uses. Their target sectors include energy, agriculture and water, real estate, and transport.

The RBF strives for transparency to promote accountability and knowledge-sharing, including by periodically providing updates on our approach to assessing the nonfinancial outcomes of our mission-aligned investing. Our mission-aligned investment strategy mandates that all our investments meet market-rate return objectives and risk attributes, supporting the idea that what is positive for people and planet can also be positive for the bottom line.  

We shared an initial report of our ESG and impact managers in 2018; since then, our assessment approach has continued to evolve. Besides financial returns, we measure our impact and ESG portfolios against several commonly used assessment tools: Impact Management Project’s Five Dimensions of Impact, the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals (UN SDGs), and Global Impact Investing Network’s IRIS+ System. 

We now present the key findings of our most recent assessment based on our portfolio as of September 2025:  

  • The RBF’s commitment to impact funds represented 23.3 percent of the endowment, surpassing the 20 percent target we set in 2016. The Fund’s commitments to impact funds has focused on the transition to a low-carbon economy (17.1 percent of the RBF’s commitment). 

Image courtesy of Spearmint Energy.

  • The RBF’s investments in ESG funds that align with the Fund’s philanthropic vision represented 13.9 percent of the endowment. Since the ESG investing industry has not yet coalesced around a standard set of metrics, the RBF measures its portfolio against the United Nations’ Sustainable Development goals. The Fund’s ESG portfolio is currently aligned with 15 of the 17 UN SDGs, and its impact portfolio is currently aligned with all 17.  
  • The RBF partners with Cerity Partners OCIO to implement and report on RBF’s shareholder engagement and proxy voting, which provide meaningful opportunities for participation in governance and institutional decision making of publicly owned corporations. The Fund’s custom proxy voting policy aligns with our mission and is implemented across the Global Equities portfolio. The RBF utilized Institutional Shareholder Services, Inc. (ISS) through 2025, and in 2026 moved to a partnership with iconik for all proxy voting needs.
  • The RBF’s portfolio and, therefore, its impact assessments, have a global reach.

Partnering with peers, our investment committee, and our OCIO, the RBF will continuously evolve and improve how we look at the nonfinancial return of our investment portfolio and will continue to share learnings publicly.

Read our full 2025 Impact Assessment Report for additional information and disclosures.

Information is provided for information purposes only and is not an offer to sell, or a solicitation of an offer to purchase, any interests in any underlying pooled vehicles or managers named therein. Holdings are subject to change.

Like many summer camps, mornings at Cazadero Music Camp in Northern California start with reveille. Unlike most camps, Caz often remixes the classic wake-up call — maybe with a brass ensemble, or oboes impersonating bagpipes, or banging on pots and pans with kitchen utensils. Since almost everyone on site, from staff to students, is a musician, the possibilities are endless. It’s the first of many musical moments Cazadero campers experience every day.  

Next year, Cazadero celebrates its 70th anniversary. Since becoming a nonprofit in the 1990s, the camp has inspired nearly 30,000 student musicians, supported by a decades-long partnership with the Hewlett Foundation. Located in a redwood forest, Caz welcomes kids ages 9 to 18 to make music while enjoying classic summer camp fun. Campers return year after year to grow as musicians and make lifelong friends, and many return as alumni to serve as staff.  

“At Hewlett, we believe that connecting Bay Area communities to the performing arts begins by bringing those experiences to our youngest neighbors,” said Tom DeCaigny, Program Officer on Hewlett’s Performing Arts team.  

Cazadero’s Executive Director Emily Wainacht knows the benefits of youth arts programs personally; she’s a Cazadero alum who credits the camp with her lifelong commitment to music.  

“There was a period when I was on the verge of quitting music entirely,” recalls Wainacht. “Caz changed that. Surrounded by an incredible community of peers and inspiring teachers who brought such joy and excitement to playing, that short time at camp gave me the purpose and drive to keep going all year long.”

Wainacht spent five years at Caz as a camper before returning as a counselor and eventually becoming Executive Director. But this summer was unlike any she’d experienced before.  

A storm and a deadline 

In December 2025, Cazadero was hit by a major storm. On Christmas Eve, Wainacht started receiving alarming texts from Camp Director Carolyn Niehaus-Owen, including photos of devastating damage. Cazadero is located in one of the rainiest parts of California, so the camp is used to storms, landslides, and floods — but nothing had compared to this.  

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Cazadero Music Camp (@cazmusiccamp)

“I went up shortly after Christmas…the pictures couldn’t even do it justice. There were branches everywhere, and the force of the branches falling and the wind had caused punctures to decks and incredible amounts of damage,” said Wainacht. “It was awful to see and hard to imagine it looking like Caz again.”  

Already halfway through the off-season, she and her team only had a few months to get camp ready. It was a big job. Still, the team was determined to open for their full 2026 camp season. “We immediately started making plans and figuring out the next steps,” said Wainacht. “Always with the goal in mind of safely opening for our first program in May. That was always the goal for us.” 

To meet that target, the team started rebuilding immediately. It was an intensive process, involving a lot of logistics between the City of Berkeley — which is Cazadero’s landlord — insurance companies, and contractors. Slowly and carefully, they started chipping away at the damage and debris while sharing regular updates with their camp community online.  

Things started feeling more normal by the time Cazadero hosted its volunteer weekend in April — an annual pre-summer tradition that took on a new meaning in the wake of the storm damage. Volunteers helped with standard opening tasks, like setting up bed frames and tarps for tents, and that’s when it was finally clear they would open as scheduled. The turnout was also a reminder of how many people care about Caz, with alumni, former staff, and neighbors all showing up to help.  

A summer of music, against the odds 

This summer, Cazadero welcomed 645 campers and employed 147 staff, none of whom would have been able to attend if camp wasn’t ready to open. Campers spent several hours a day in music classes, learning new pieces in only a few days, studying under different conductors, and performing concerts every week for a live audience. All of them share one thing: a commitment to their craft. As one camper described it: “Everyone speaks the same language. Not the language of English, Spanish, or French, but the language of music.” 

Wainacht also pointed to the broader value of sleepaway camp itself, whether campers spend their days studying instruments, playing sports, or simply soaking up the summer sun.  

“In a world increasingly driven toward isolation and screens, camp gives young people this incredible opportunity to connect and collaborate together, in person. And we’re in this canyon in a redwood forest with no cell reception,” she said. “They’re fully present in the work of the camp and the communities that they are building.” 

DeCaigny said, “Whether someone dreams of a career in music or simply enjoys playing as a hobby, I have seen firsthand the impact Caz has on campers. It shows the power of music to bring people together while helping young people become more creative, confident, and connected to their communities.” 

Cazadero just closed out another successful summer. Looking back, Wainacht can recall countless memories that made the long hours of cleanup and complicated logistics more than worth it, but one in particular stands out: a shy student whose stage fright was so severe he ran off stage during an earlier school concert. This summer, he joined Cazadero’s jazz ensemble and conquered his fears by opting to perform not once but twice at the weekly concert.  

“At Caz, he found that joy in music again.”

Cazadero’s Executive Director Emily Wainacht knows the benefits of youth arts programs personally; she’s a Cazadero alum who credits the camp with her lifelong commitment to music.  

“There was a period when I was on the verge of quitting music entirely,” recalls Wainacht. “Caz changed that. Surrounded by an incredible community of peers and inspiring teachers who brought such joy and excitement to playing, that short time at camp gave me the purpose and drive to keep going all year long.”

Wainacht spent five years at Caz as a camper before returning as a counselor and eventually becoming Executive Director. But this summer was unlike any she’d experienced before.  

A storm and a deadline 

In December 2025, Cazadero was hit by a major storm. On Christmas Eve, Wainacht started receiving alarming texts from Camp Director Carolyn Niehaus-Owen, including photos of devastating damage. Cazadero is located in one of the rainiest parts of California, so the camp is used to storms, landslides, and floods — but nothing had compared to this.  

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Cazadero Music Camp (@cazmusiccamp)

“I went up shortly after Christmas…the pictures couldn’t even do it justice. There were branches everywhere, and the force of the branches falling and the wind had caused punctures to decks and incredible amounts of damage,” said Wainacht. “It was awful to see and hard to imagine it looking like Caz again.”  

Already halfway through the off-season, she and her team only had a few months to get camp ready. It was a big job. Still, the team was determined to open for their full 2026 camp season. “We immediately started making plans and figuring out the next steps,” said Wainacht. “Always with the goal in mind of safely opening for our first program in May. That was always the goal for us.” 

To meet that target, the team started rebuilding immediately. It was an intensive process, involving a lot of logistics between the City of Berkeley — which is Cazadero’s landlord — insurance companies, and contractors. Slowly and carefully, they started chipping away at the damage and debris while sharing regular updates with their camp community online.  

Things started feeling more normal by the time Cazadero hosted its volunteer weekend in April — an annual pre-summer tradition that took on a new meaning in the wake of the storm damage. Volunteers helped with standard opening tasks, like setting up bed frames and tarps for tents, and that’s when it was finally clear they would open as scheduled. The turnout was also a reminder of how many people care about Caz, with alumni, former staff, and neighbors all showing up to help.  

A summer of music, against the odds 

This summer, Cazadero welcomed 645 campers and employed 147 staff, none of whom would have been able to attend if camp wasn’t ready to open. Campers spent several hours a day in music classes, learning new pieces in only a few days, studying under different conductors, and performing concerts every week for a live audience. All of them share one thing: a commitment to their craft. As one camper described it: “Everyone speaks the same language. Not the language of English, Spanish, or French, but the language of music.” 

Wainacht also pointed to the broader value of sleepaway camp itself, whether campers spend their days studying instruments, playing sports, or simply soaking up the summer sun.  

“In a world increasingly driven toward isolation and screens, camp gives young people this incredible opportunity to connect and collaborate together, in person. And we’re in this canyon in a redwood forest with no cell reception,” she said. “They’re fully present in the work of the camp and the communities that they are building.” 

DeCaigny said, “Whether someone dreams of a career in music or simply enjoys playing as a hobby, I have seen firsthand the impact Caz has on campers. It shows the power of music to bring people together while helping young people become more creative, confident, and connected to their communities.” 

Cazadero just closed out another successful summer. Looking back, Wainacht can recall countless memories that made the long hours of cleanup and complicated logistics more than worth it, but one in particular stands out: a shy student whose stage fright was so severe he ran off stage during an earlier school concert. This summer, he joined Cazadero’s jazz ensemble and conquered his fears by opting to perform not once but twice at the weekly concert.  

“At Caz, he found that joy in music again.”

The 2026 Goalkeepers Report looks at the extraordinary potential of artificial intelligence to improve health, education, and well-being in communities around the world, and it underlines what it will take to ensure that this rapidly evolving technology benefits everyone.

Global progress is real but fragile.

Over the past 25 years, investments in people, innovation, and tools that save lives have driven extraordinary progress. Deaths from HIV, polio, tuberculosis, and malaria have all fallen significantly, and millions more people have had healthier lives and more opportunity.

But continued gains are not guaranteed. In some places, progress has already slowed, and recent cuts to global health funding are putting hard-won advances at risk.

AI could help accelerate progress, and in some places it already has.

If AI is built to support people everywhere, it could help life-changing knowledge and support travel faster and farther, leading to better health, education, and economic opportunity. We already see signs of what that could look like across education, health care, and agriculture.

The window to shape who benefits from AI is short.

AI is developing quickly, and the decisions made in the next 12 to 18 months—about how it is built, funded, and deployed—could determine whether its benefits reach people everywhere or remain concentrated among those who already have the most access and resources. 

Making AI work for everyone will take more than better technology.

For AI to benefit everyone, three things are important: AI tools need to work in every language people speak. They need to be grounded in local data and built for local realities. And countries and communities need the expertise and access to shape and use these tools themselves. Today these things are far from universal, but if we can get them right, AI has a better chance of reaching the people who stand to benefit most—and becoming a tool for faster, more equitable progress. 

AI tools should support people, not replace them.

AI is most powerful when it supports people rather than replaces them—giving a health worker another source of insight, helping a teacher better understand what each student needs, or getting useful information to a farmer at the right moment. When AI empowers people to solve tough problems, it can strengthen their decision-making and help progress move faster.

The path forward for AI is still a choice. AI can reinforce gaps that already exist or, if it is deliberately built for people everywhere, it can help accelerate progress and expand economic opportunity. 

Read the 2026 Goalkeepers Report for more on how AI could help build a more equitable world.

Gouden enveloppen vallen natuurlijk meteen op. Een gloednieuwe BMW blijkbaar iets minder. Op postcode 9351 DA in Leek verrast Gaston de winnaars met de PostcodeStraatprijs. En Greet? Die moet nog even goed om zich heen kijken om haar extra verrassing te ontdekken.

woensdag 16 september 2026 - Winnaarsverhalen

 Zo vader, zo dochter

Jan en Antje genieten van het mooie weer in hun tuin als Gaston langskomt. Als ze horen dat ze € 25.000,- winnen, kan Antje het bijna niet geloven. "Wauw, net als mijn vader! Hij won in 2009 ook de PostcodeStraatprijs."Het stel weet al wat ze met het geld willen doen. Het huis krijgt een opfrisbeurt met nieuw behang en een lik verf. 

Nog maar een weekje weg? 

Bij Douwe en Debbie staat de auto nog vol vakantiebagage voor de deur. Ze komen net terug van een week op Ameland. Maar na het zien van de cheque van € 25.000,- begint het alweer te kriebelen. "Ik denk dat we nog een week vakantie gaan boeken. Misschien dit keer wel naar een ander Waddeneiland." 

Mensen helpen

Hosein ontvangt een cheque van € 25.000,-. Hij hoeft niet lang na te denken over de bestemming van zijn prijs. "Ik wil mensen helpen", zegt hij resoluut. Op de vraag van Gaston hoe hij dat wil doen, antwoordt hij: "Ik kom uit Iran. Daar wil ik de mensen helpen die te maken hebben met de oorlog." 

Waar staat de auto dan? 

Greet is heel blij met haar € 25.000,-, al weet ze nog niet wat ze ermee gaat doen. Dan blijkt Gaston nóg iets voor haar te hebben. Hij haalt de sleutels van een gloednieuwe BMW tevoorschijn. Ze zag de auto eerst even niet staan, maar na het omdraaien schrikt ze lachend. Ze is heel erg blij!

Dit gebeurde nog nooit in de 26-jarige geschiedenis van Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht. Joey uit Waddinxveen geeft in de eerste ronde bij 3 van de 5 vragen als snelste het goede antwoord. Daarmee pakt hij een plek achter de desk, wint hij € 10.000,- én een gloednieuwe BMW. En zijn bijzondere avond gaat verder. Joey bereikt ook de finale en wint daar maar liefst € 130.000,-. 

woensdag 16 september 2026 - Winnaarsverhalen

Meespelen én een koffer kiezen

Het begint al in de eerste ronde, bij de tweede vraag. Joey geeft als snelste het juiste antwoord en verovert een plek achter de desk. Even later is hij wéér de snelste. Dit keer kiest hij voor een koffer. Daarin zit € 10.000,-. 

Nog een koffer te openen

En dan gebeurt het nóg een keer. Bij de laatste vraag reageert Joey opnieuw als snelste. “Dit hebben we echt nog nooit meegemaakt”, zegt Linda de Mol verbaasd. Zijn 3e succes levert hem een gloednieuwe BMW op.

Joey bereikt de finale 

Maar Joey’s avond is nog lang niet voorbij. Hij bereikt de finale en speelt daar voor de grote geldbedragen. Uiteindelijk accepteert hij bij een bod van € 130.000,- voor zekerheid. “Soms moet je accepteren dat het genoeg is.” 
 

Wat gaat Joey doen met zijn prijzen?

€ 130.000,-, € 10.000,- én een nieuwe BMW op één avond. Denise vat het mooi samen: “Het is net alsof we in een droom leven”, zegt Denise, de partner van Joey. Met het geld willen Joey en Denise hun huis verbouwen en mooie reizen maken met hun gezin en familie.

Kijk jij volgende zondag mee?

Tussen 6 september en 18 oktober 2026 geniet je iedere zondag om 19:55 uur van Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht op SBS6. Wil je Postcode Loterij Miljoenenjacht terugkijken? Dat kan via KIJK.nl.
